<meta>This entry describes the physical exterior and binding of the manuscript Regina latinus 1344, serving as the introduction to the digital transcription of this volume.</meta>

# Vatican Library, Manuscript Regina latinus 1344

->**Exterior Binding**<-

This manuscript is preserved in a fine **leather binding** <term>binding: the protective cover and the process of securing the pages together</term>. The leather is a deep reddish-brown with a visible grainy texture, suggesting a high-quality historical craftsmanship. 

The front cover is adorned with a decorative **gold-tooled** <term>gold-tooled: a technique where decorative patterns are pressed into leather using heated metal stamps and gold leaf</term> border. This border consists of a repeating pattern of small interlocking circles or chain-like links, which catch the light and frame the volume.

The **spine** <term>spine: the back edge of the book where the pages are joined</term> is constructed with several **raised bands** <term>raised bands: horizontal ridges along the spine that cover the structural cords used to sew the book's sections together</term>. While the original gold lettering on the spine has become difficult to read over the centuries, a modern white library label has been attached, clearly identifying the book's location in the collection:

->**Reg. lat. 1344**<-

<note>original: "Reg. lat. 1344" — This abbreviation stands for *Reginensis latinus 1344*. It indicates that this book was once part of the personal collection of Queen Christina of Sweden (1626–1689), whose manuscripts were eventually acquired by the Vatican Library.</note>

A faint watermark from the Vatican Apostolic Library is visible across the center of the cover, a mark of its current home in Rome.

<summary>This page describes the ornate leather and gold-tooled binding of manuscript Regina latinus 1344, formerly belonging to Queen Christina of Sweden.</summary>
<keywords>binding, leather, gold-tooled, spine, library label, Queen Christina of Sweden, Vatican Library, Reginensis latinus</keywords>

<unclear>Year 1597</unclear>
<unclear>January 25th</unclear> <note>original: "VIII. Cal. Feb." — The 8th day before the Kalends of February.</note>
<unclear>From the books of Mancini</unclear>

# THE STEGANOGRAPHY OF JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS, BOOK ONE
# TO THE MOST SERENE PRINCE, LORD PHILIP, COUNT PALATINE OF THE RHINE, DUKE OF BAVARIA
->and Elector of the Holy Empire, etc.<-

It is the opinion of the most learned men that the most ancient sages—whom people are accustomed to calling *philosophers* <note>original: "philosophos," a term of Greek origin meaning "lovers of wisdom."</note> in the Greek tongue—whenever they discovered any secrets <term>arcana</term><note>Secrets or hidden mysteries of nature or divine knowledge.</note> of either nature or of Art, they hid them in various ways and figures. This was done so that such knowledge would not fall into the awareness of wicked men. The teachers of the Jews also confirm that Moses, that most famous leader of the Israelite people, did not reveal the ineffable and secret mysteries in simple words when he wrote his description of the Creation of Heaven and Earth. Among our own most learned and holy men, Dionysius <note>Likely referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian mystic and theologian.</note> and seven <note>The number 7 here may refer to a specific group of scholars or be a scribal abbreviation for "others."</note> others affirm that nearly innumerable mysteries lie hidden within the *Apocalypse of John* <note>The biblical Book of Revelation.</note>. The sages of the Greeks, who were held in no small esteem by their own people, did exactly the same.

Furthermore, our own seven philosophers and most learned poets did the same; by devoting their efforts to preserving fables, they used a clever invention to ensure that, through the same narrative, they handed down one meaning to the uninitiated and another to the truly learned. Because of the slowness of my own wit, I am unable to imitate these most zealous lovers of wisdom; nevertheless, I do not cease to admire them and to read them with the greatest diligence as I am able. For when I consider that they, as the most skillful of men, devised such great things through their own study, I constrain myself by a certain force to "grow warm" <note>An idiom for becoming inspired or passionate.</note>; I am driven toward some kind of imitation of those who went before, even if I am among the most recent of their followers. Nor has this opinion entirely deceived me, I believe; for it was then that I learned those things which I had previously desired through a continuous study of reading. I have now unlocked an entry for the reader to investigate more secret and intimate mysteries through my own thoughts. For even if no—

<meta>This page continues Trithemius's preface, moving from historical examples of secrecy to the justification for his own "Steganography." He explains that his system is designed to be incomprehensible to the uninitiated, requiring a direct transmission of knowledge from teacher to student, which he likens to the Hebrew tradition of Kabbalah.</meta>

...[is of] such erudition or diligence <term>industria</term><note>In this context, it refers to purposeful hard work and systematic application of skill.</note> that I might be able or dare to profess that I have followed that ancient method of the sages <term>sapientum</term><note>The wise men or philosophers of antiquity.</note> for concealing mysteries <term>misteria</term><note>Hidden religious or philosophical truths.</note> in every part. However, I have discovered certain similar and varied modes, which seem to me to be shaped so that I may communicate the most secret intentions of my mind to another. I have fashioned this art of writing by which I can convey whatever I wish most widely, without illusion, suspicion, or detection by anyone, through open messengers or letters.

And this new invention of a most secret art, I have brought together into this very volume—not without the greatest labors—solely at the instance of the Most Serene Prince, Lord Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, and Prince Elector of the Holy Roman Empire. He is ever the most munificent and the wisest of all philosophers in his heart, and no one has seemed more worthy to me; thus, I have deservedly commended this great secret to be revealed to him. 

Lest it should reach those who are not friends, or the common crowd of the unskillful or wicked men, I consider it a significant part of my duty to ensure that—since this work teaches mysteries—it should be so inaccessible to those reporting it that no one from the number of the unskillful (no one, I say, unless he be most learned) can perfectly penetrate the secrets <term>arcanisma</term><note>The most hidden or "arcane" parts of a science.</note> of this science to the full extent of our intention, except through reception from a teacher. This the Hebrews call **Kabbalah** <note>original: "Cabalam," a Hebrew term meaning "tradition" or "reception." Trithemius uses it here to describe a system of knowledge passed orally from master to student to ensure it remains secret.</note>, which is set over the most hidden mysteries.

Nor would the knowledge of this most secret art, if divulged to the wicked and the reprobate <term>reprobos</term><note>Those rejected by God or lacking moral principle; the "unworthy."</note>, harm the Commonwealth <note>original: "Reipub:" an abbreviation for "Res publica."</note> any less than it would benefit the good. For indeed, just, good, and truth-seeking men use all inventions for good and for common utility; likewise, the evil and the reprobate hunt for opportunities to become worse not only from bad things, but even from good and most holy institutions. Beware, therefore, lest it happen that this most secret and otherwise useful invention of our Art, given to the Commonwealth, [falls into the wrong hands]. For just as it offers itself as an instrument to good and most holy men for the best [purposes...]

<meta>This page continues Trithemius's justification for the secrecy of his work. He transitions from warning about the dangers of the "unskillful" possessing this knowledge to describing the practical applications and the absolute security of his cryptographic system, which he claims can even disguise messages as simple, innocent Latin prose.</meta>

<margin>In this way, it might offer a service <term>ministerium</term><note>A functional role or a means of providing assistance; here, the author warns that his art could be misused by the wicked.</note> for wicked deeds to the perverse and the impious.</margin> For those who are just, good, and lovers of honor can signify the fruit of their will—whether for a private or common good—to another who knows this art, whenever and as often as he wishes to know it, perfectly, copiously, and with complete integrity, without any suspicion from any mortal, through open messengers or letters, whether they be open or sealed. So it is that no one, however learned or curious, may be able to suspect anything of the sender’s secret. Nor, even if they should suspect it, can they at any time detect it. And so, even through slippery and malicious connections, yet using Latin words everywhere once this art has been written down, one will be able to master it without a teacher in two days at the most.

From now on, one will write letters in the Latin language with proper composition, using any open narrative, beautiful and sufficiently ornate; and to me or to another skilled in this art, they will convey the secret of their will <note>original: "voluntatis suae arcanum"</note>... wrapped in fated mysteries by the power of the Kabbalah <term>Cabalistica</term><note>Referring to the Jewish mystical tradition. Trithemius uses this term to suggest that his method of encoding messages relies on a hidden, spiritual, or mathematical logic similar to how Kabbalists interpreted sacred texts.</note>, so that no one—no matter how learned or studious—is able to penetrate them without the spirits of this art of which I am about to speak.

From now on, the learned and the unlearned, man and woman, boy and old man, good and bad, public official and private citizen, will write in Latin or in any other language; thus everywhere, through all the climates of the world, they will write letters in Latin, Greek, or foreign <term>barbaras</term><note>Meaning languages other than Latin or Greek, such as vernacular German or other regional tongues, which were often labeled "barbarous" by Renaissance humanists.</note> tongues, free from all suspicion. To those who do not know the art, one thing is shown openly, while to those who know it, another is shown in secret. Nor would the faith contracted by the sacrament <term>sacramentum</term><note>The religious rite of marriage, emphasizing the gravity of the secret communication.</note> between spouses remain safe among the wicked once this science is made public. While a wife, though hitherto ignorant of the Latin language, through simple <note>original: "puerilia"</note> words, honest and most holy, in any language or idiom, now sufficiently...

<summary>Trithemius describes his "Steganography" as a perfectly secure method of communication that can disguise secrets within seemingly innocent, ornate Latin letters. He claims the art is so effective that even those unlearned in Latin can use it, though he warns it must be kept from the wicked to prevent the subversion of social and religious bonds like marriage.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Trithemius's argument regarding the potential dangers of his "Steganography." words, he could most broadly understand the evil and **shameless** <note>original: "impudica"</note> mind and intention of an adulterous or fornicating lover, even while the husband is present and praising the letters as excellent; and he could send back his desire in the same way, as broadly and copiously as he wished, most secretly in the same or other letters in a beautiful and sufficiently ornate sequence. 

And although this knowledge is in itself excellent and useful enough to the **State** <term>Reipublicae</term><note>original: "Reipub:". Referring to the common good or the organized political community.</note>, nevertheless, if it should come to the knowledge of the wicked (which God forbid), the order of the entire State could, in the course of time, be not slightly disturbed, and public trust endangered. All letters, legal instruments, records, and finally even the very conversations of men would be turned into the gravest suspicion. No one would then believe any letters, however sacred and honest, without fear; trust would rarely be given to epistles. Because no matter how honest and modest the words might be, it would always be thought that trickery, fraud, and deception lay beneath; and men would become so fearful, no less toward friends than toward adversaries, as to be full of suspicion. 

Nor could anyone, even if he lived for a thousand years, become so learned and expert in this secret teaching of writing that there would not remain for others infinite ways of writing curiously, most hiddenly, and most secretly in this very art, and—by working according to the will of any expert—extending to all present things which he himself, with his teacher, has not yet grasped. 

For since the sharp spirits, both good and evil, created by the Most High God for our service and obedience—through whose intelligence all holy artistic things are revealed—are infinite in number to us, and the good spirits are incomprehensible in their own ways, so this art of ours, which we call **Steganography** <term>Steganographia</term><note>A term coined by Trithemius, from the Greek *steganos* (covered/secret) and *graphe* (writing).</note> or secret writings and **mysteries** <term>misteria</term>, can never be fully known for all eternity in all its modes, differences, qualities, and operations by any mortal (however much they may excel in judgment or erudition, for the holy things contained in it are perfect).

<summary>Trithemius warns that while Steganography is a noble art, its misuse by the wicked could destroy social trust and public order; he further claims the art is so vast and spiritually deep that it can never be fully exhausted by human study.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Trithemius's introduction to his system of secret writing. Having previously warned about the potential for misuse by the wicked, he now transitions into a defense of the depth of this "science" and, crucially, a legal and religious disclaimer to protect himself from accusations of heresy or black magic.</meta>

...a contradiction can occur. For in this science there is a most profound and infinite **chaos** <note>original: "chaos infinitum altissimum." In this context, it refers to a vast, inexhaustible depth of knowledge rather than mere confusion.</note> that no one can perfectly comprehend. Because no matter how learned and expert one might be in this art, he always grasps less than what still remains to be learned.

For this deep and most secret art has this quality: it renders the student incomparably more learned than the teacher—provided he is naturally inclined to perceive such things, especially in those matters handed down by **Cabalistic tradition** <term>traditione Cabalistica</term> <note>Johannes Trithemius often blended cryptographic techniques with the terminology of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah), using the idea of hidden meanings within text.</note>.

But lest any future reader of this art—when encountering the names, offices, ranks, distinctions, properties, prayers, and any other operations of **spirits** <note>Trithemius famously masked his cryptographic codes as "spirit conjurations" to hide their true nature, which led to centuries of controversy over whether his work was magic or science.</note>, through whose intelligences all the secrets of this science are delivered and revealed—should believe or think that I have practiced **Necromancy** <term>Necromantiam</term> <note>The forbidden practice of communicating with the dead or summoning demons.</note> and magic, or entered into a pact with **Demons**, or used any other superstition, I have deemed it necessary and timely to clear my reputation and name from such an envious blemish, fault, and stain. I do this through a solemn declaration of truth in this prologue, claiming my rightful standing.

I declare, therefore, before Almighty God, from whom nothing can be hidden, and before **JESUS CHRIST** his only-begotten Son, who shall judge the living and the dead: I say in truth, and indeed I testify, that each and every thing I have said in this work, or shall say hereafter—all properties of this science or art, the methods, figures, operations, traditions, receptions, formations, inventions, institutions, alterations, and everything pertaining to its theory, discovery, writing, operation, and practice, whether in part or in whole—and all that is contained in this volume of ours, rests upon true Catholic and natural principles. Everything is done with God, with a good conscience, without harm to the Christian faith, with the integrity of Church tradition, without any superstition, without **idolatry** <term>idololatria</term>, and without any pact with evil spirits, ex-

<meta>This page continues Trithemius’s formal "protestation" or declaration of faith. He is explicitly denying that his secret methods involve demonic magic, positioning himself as a loyal Benedictine monk and a faithful Catholic to avoid the Inquisition’s reach.</meta>

...explicitly and implicitly: without fumigation <note>original: "suffumigatione." The practice of burning incense or herbs to summon or appease spirits, common in ritual magic.</note>, adoration, veneration, worship, sacrifice, or offerings to demons, and without any fault or sin, whether venial or mortal <note>In Catholic theology, venial sins are minor offenses, while mortal sins are grave actions that sever one's relationship with God.</note>. Let all things and each individual part be done with truth, rectitude, sincerity, and purity. And let it be known that the knowledge and practice of this invention does not lead to good use except for a wise man, a Christian, and a faithful person. 

For I too am a Christian and of the monastic life <note>original: "monasticae conversationis." This refers to the specific way of life and conduct required of a monk.</note>, voluntarily devoted to it, and I desire to live and conduct myself in no other way than what becomes a true Christian and a monk professed under the Rule of God the father **St. Benedict** <note>St. Benedict of Nursia (c. 480–547), the founder of Western monasticism. Trithemius was the Abbot of the Benedictine monastery at Sponheim.</note>. I have received the Catholic faith itself according to the tradition of the **Holy Roman Church**, in which I was baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. This faith I hold and believe along with the universal Church, and as long as I live, with God’s help, I intend to always keep it inviolate and firm in my heart, my speech, and my deeds. 

Far be it from me to deviate from it on any occasion. May it be far from me to say or teach anything that is contrary to Christian faith and piety, harmful to holy morals, or in any way adverse to the most proven Rule. I fear God and invoke Him in His worship, from whom I shall not be separated, neither living nor dead. 

I have placed this declaration <term>protestationem</term> of mine at the beginning of this work for you not without cause: because I know many are suspicious. When they are unable to understand the things that are written, they turn to envy our good and holy studies; they are ready to complain and nitpick <note>original: "cavillaturi." To raise trivial or annoying objections.</note> with evil arts and superstitious inventions. 

And therefore, to those who are most pious and to all whoever will read these observations <term>sumptomata</term> <note>While "symptomata" usually means symptoms, Trithemius uses it here to mean the various parts or "phenomena" of his cryptographic system.</note> of ours, we earnestly pray: that if they understand this holy tradition of ours, they keep it hidden within their own circles. Do not pour out such pure mysteries into the public. But if they do not understand them (since we know of none who do), let them learn before they condemn. For he rightly shows himself to be envious who, before he has known the truth of the cause, brings forth a sentence of accusation. Learn this art first, and afterwards judge; because if you deserve to understand, you will not [condemn] it...

He warns readers to keep his methods secret and to learn the system fully before accusing him of heresy or magic.</summary>

# CHAPTER ONE

In this first chapter of this first book is contained the method and operation by the principal spirit **PAMERSIEL**, [along with] Amoyr and Madriel, through the minister **EBRASATHEAN**, [and] Abrahel, Torafiel, Nazros, Ormenus, Itiller, Ration, and Namorpheiel. To this let there be a commission with all [things]. In this first chapter there is a very difficult and peril-filled operation on account of <note>original: "pp." or "propter."</note> the pride and rebellion of its spirits, who do not yield to anyone unless he is most expert in this art. For to novices and those less proven <note>original: "pbatis" or "probatis."</note> in this art, they not only do not obey, but even if they are urged too much, they frequently harm them and offend them with various illusions. They are cursed and unfaithful beyond all other aerial spirits <note>In the medieval worldview, "aerial spirits" were thought to inhabit the air between Earth and the Moon; Trithemius uses them here as metaphors for the carriers of his secret messages.</note>: and they obey no one at all unless compelled by the greatest oaths, and according to what is committed to them, they often unfaithfully reveal [it] to others. For as soon as they have been sent out with our letters to him to whom they are sent, bursting in without order—like people fleeing from battle without a leader—they hasten furiously, and filling the air with their shouting, they often reveal secrets even before the sight of the sender. We advise, therefore, that no one in this art of operation should compel these [spirits], nor seek their ministries or help. Because they are headstrong and unfaithful, whereas one can find many others among those we shall speak of later who are quite benevolent. These offer themselves voluntarily, ready for obedience. If anyone, however, wishes to experience their headstrong nature and test those things which we have said...

<summary>Trithemius begins the first chapter of his work by introducing the spirit Pamersiel and his subordinates, warning the reader that these particular "spirits" are rebellious, dangerous for beginners, and prone to revealing secrets prematurely.</summary>
<keywords>Pamersiel, Ebrasathean, aerial spirits, cryptography, secret messages, occult warnings, Johannes Trithemius</keywords>

<margin>Take note</margin>
Consider carefully all things which we have said in the present chapter, and you will be able to understand more easily those things which we are about to say in the following ones. And so that we may prove what we have said with an example, let us set down our intention in the common tongue, or if it pleases, in Latin, which we will subsequently make known to a friend in the manner aforesaid. In this way, this mental intention may serve the purpose of some prince who wishes his absent vassal to know his mind.

> To our sincere and faithful subject: For just causes, we have decreed that the City of Strasbourg <note>original: *Argentinensem*</note> is to be invaded and attacked with a very great army and power on the upcoming feast of Saints Vitus and Modestus <note>June 15th</note>. Therefore we desire of you, that by the oath and loyalty of your service, by which you are bound to us, you appear on the aforementioned day, armed to your utmost ability, at the fourth hour after noon before the aforesaid City, in a forest not far distant from it. And there, await our decision on whatever else needs to be done. Nor should you reveal this plan of ours to any man; because this, being mercifully and kindly accepted by you, we shall reward with our favor.

To make known this secret to the vassal with such an intention of the sender, let them be written thus, or in another way.

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for sending secret messages via spiritual intermediaries. Having provided a sample military letter about Strasbourg on the previous page, the author now provides a "pious" prayer to serve as the overt cover text and begins to explain the ritual directions and locations of the spirits involved.</meta>

Almighty eternal God, who created all things out of nothing, have mercy on us, through the most loving passion of your only-begotten son dying on the cross. Who was conceived of the Holy Spirit without male intervention. Born of the most pure ever-virgin Mary, and voluntarily delivered into death for us. Hear us, etc. <note>original: *Exaudi &c.* This prayer serves as a "cover" text; to a casual reader, the letter appears to be a common religious devotion.</note>

Use a simple and open narrative of this kind, or any other you wish, which all who read it will understand. It is useful because it contains no secret <note>at least not on the surface</note>, and you would not fear it coming into anyone's sight. # CHAPTER IV
<margin>ASELIEL</margin>
The prince of the fourth chapter is Aseliel, who dwells toward the South-Southeast <note>original: "Euro Austrum"; a classical wind direction between the East and the South</note>. He has under him 30 substitute princes with their own servants. He presides over those matters which pertain to love.

The great Prince **ASELIEL** holds the fourth mansion from the east toward the South-Southeast with his spirits. Of these, ten serve daytime operations in this art, and twenty serve the nighttime ones. The power and duty of all these spirits is to report those matters which pertain to the love of women. These thirty principal spirits have others under them, and they send just as many others in order to fulfill their duties when they have been called by the practitioner in the proper manner. Again, there are others subject to these, of whom there is a great number. Rather, one or two suffice, whether the operation is for the night or the day. You do not need more unless the operation is for diverse matters.

<margin>Example</margin>
Let us imagine the secret of your mind is such: You have a lady friend for whose love you are dying, and she no less for yours, but neither of you dare to speak or approach one another because of the watchfulness of the elders <note>Likely referring to strict parents or guardians</note>. # CHAPTER SIX
The supreme prince of this chapter is **Gediel**, who has his dwelling in the South. Subject to him are twenty other princes by day and as many by night, along with their servants. The duty <note>original: "officium"</note> of these spirits is to report everything pertaining to the reconciliation of a friend regarding any imminent danger—especially concerning a prince and the defense of the fatherland, camps, and cities—and to provide everything that benefits friends and the carrying out of these matters for their well-being. This applies as well to actions taken against enemies and adversaries.

# CHAPTER SEVEN
The supreme prince of this chapter is **Asyriel**, whose dwelling is in the Southwest <note>original: "Africum"; referring to the wind blowing from the direction of Africa, which to the Romans represented the Southwest</note>. He has under his dominion twenty leaders <note>original: "duces"</note> who are Lords of the day, and as many for the night. Their duty is to report the counsels of promised friends. All these leaders have such a close relationship with one another that when the practitioner <note>original: "operator"; the ritual magician performing the work</note> speaks to them, they immediately send out their servants; indeed, they come in person to hear the commissions. When the practitioner ceases speaking to the princes, the servants are seen to stand ready once again.

He goes to that person, delivers the message faithfully, and if anything is entrusted back to you, he brings it home.

# CHAPTER XVII

The principal spirit and supreme Emperor is called **CARNESIEL**, and he dwells in the East, having under him many dukes, princes, and servants. Their duty is to report all things that are sent toward the East. Since, in truth, many and varied human affairs may arise that need to be made known, and as there is nothing in the aforementioned 16 mansions <note>Referring to the 16 previous chapters/sections describing specific spirit residences</note> described thus far that is designated for signaling via friendly spirits, these four were found by the author's diligence. This was done so that those practicing this art of **Steganography** <term>Steganography: From the Greek *steganos* (hidden) and *graphein* (writing). In Trithemius's context, it refers to a method of secret communication disguised as magic.</term> might encounter no difficulty regarding the perfection of the work. For after mention was made in the preceding chapters of certain specific spirits who presided over spiritual secrets, it now seems appropriate to introduce certain general spirits for announcing general matters. 

So that if perhaps a secret should arise that needs to be reported, for which no commission <note>original: "Commissio," meaning a specific assignment or jurisdiction</note> is found among the previously mentioned spirits, it may be referred to these spirits. They, in their own way, have authority over all things. Yet this is arranged in such a way that the general authority does not detract from the specific, nor should a specific matter that is not clearly expressed refuse the service of the general authority. Therefore, there are four great princes who, with their dukes and high-ranking subordinates, preside over the reporting of all secrets expressed above. Of these, the first, **Carnesiel**, presides over all who wish to send messages toward the East. 2. **Caspiel** toward the South, **Amenadiel** toward the West, and **Demoriel** toward the North. 

Therefore, when you wish to report any secret through friendly spirits whom you send toward the East—for I desire more of what you wish from the prince **Carnesiel** <note>The Latin phrasing "Volo enim..." appears to be the beginning of a conjuration or a command addressed to the spirit</note>—we wish you to know our art throughout the entire operation toward the eastern region of the world.

There is a certain man, evil despite an appearance of honesty, who knows that I have some influence with a friend and asks me for a letter of recommendation to him. I do not dare to refuse him. The man reads it and sees what looks like an open path for him to plot his schemes, though the actual power to do so has been taken away from him by my secret warning. He takes the letter and departs happy, in his true spirit.

I signify to Your Grace, most Illustrious Prince and Counselor <unclear>Cons.</unclear>, that once the beneficial office over the Altar of the Evangelist <note>The "Altar of the Evangelist" here is likely a code word or placeholder used in the steganographic system to hide the true intent of the message.</note> became vacant after a barren night, lest Your Grace, or those who expect the said Altar from the unskillful, provides for the fulfillment of either vow without deliberation, I pray—although I remain far unworthy—that my prayers in the sight of the greatest and noblest prince may seem to bring back some worthy benefit. # CHAPTER XXI

<margin>Geradiel</margin>
**Geradiel** is the Prince and Emperor of this chapter, dwelling in no specific region of the world but accustomed to wandering everywhere. Beside those Emperors, Princes, and Dukes of the Spirits whom we named in the preceding chapters—who reside in fixed places and are assigned according to a visible order—there are others who are everywhere wandering and unstable, settling in no place. These the ancient Sages and mages called *Droeos hierusta* <note>original: "Droeos hierusta," likely a corruption of Greek terms meaning "holy" or "sacred" aerial spirits, though Trithemius characterizes them as "vile" or lowly</note>, who are of low rank; they fly in the air like a mist <note>original: "simili misto," meaning a nebulous or mixed substance</note> without order, without habitation, and without restriction. Among these, there are some who are not useful to us for Steganography <term>Steganographia: "hidden writing," the art of sending secret messages through spiritual or cryptographic means</term>, because they do not require the observation of specific locations, but can be summoned by an incantation in any place.

The first of these is called **Geradiel**, who does not have any Duke or Prince under him, but only many—nearly innumerable—servants <term>famulos: attendant spirits or servitors</term>, whom he takes into his service according to the ranks they hold among themselves during the 24 hours of the day and night. Their general duty is to report secrets to all and any region of the world you might wish.

# CHAPTER XXII

Briel, a great prince, follows Geradiel in this chapter; he connects [others] and greatly hates, persecutes, and detests other spirits and especially [other] princes, and no less the devils [born] from them. He flees from them with all his divisions and families. Nor is he ever accustomed to come except by night, and this frequently with great horror and trembling for those performing the work—especially if they are not strong in the art, and steady and brave in spirit. He frequently appears in the **form** <gloss>original: "specie," meaning outward appearance or shape</gloss> of a serpent, having a maiden’s head, but the tail and the rest of the body of a serpent, whistling horribly. Once the human words have been taken up in the proper manner, he speaks.

He has dukes and princes under him, whom he is accustomed to send into service, along with their families and troops, whose multitude is almost innumerable. The Duke is accustomed to appear in the form we have mentioned, but the servants usually appear frequently like monkeys, or jesters, players, and dancers, leaping from on high to the ground with marvelous **imagination** <term>phantasia: In Renaissance magic, this refers to the spirit's power to create vivid, often deceptive, sensory illusions in the mind of the observer.</term>.

Their office is to report all nightly secrets during the night. They are also willing to perform service regarding prisons and places for captives; and similarly in those things which pertain to carnal love, providing fertility for lovers. And all things that are done in the night are [their concern], whether good or evil, because they hate the light.

# CHAPTER XXIII

**Hydriel** <note>The name is derived from the Greek word *hydros*, meaning water.</note> is called the supreme Prince of this chapter. He dwells in waters, among fish, in lakes, marshes, the sea, and in muddy springs, cisterns, and rivers. He holds under his dominion those spirits described above in the preceding chapter concerning their Emperor. Their general duty is to manage all things both through water and across land, whether by day or by night. He is quite willing and benevolent toward all his masters. However, they appear in a mixed form when they come under threat <note>original: "comminati," suggesting spirits summoned through forceful commands or conjurations</note>. In their lowest manifestation, they appear frequently; yet, they sometimes possess a maiden’s head that is very beautiful, with flowing hair.

# CHAPTER XXIV

**Pyrichyel** <note>The name stems from the Greek *pyr*, meaning fire.</note> has under him many princes, counts, and servants, whose number is uncertain. He does not have dukes or princes under him in the manner of the others, but only counts and sub-ministers. Otherwise, he is quite benevolent. He took his name from fire because he is frequently observed to frequent the vicinity of fire.

# CHAPTER XXV

### CHAPTER XXXII

After we have described the offices of the superior spirits in our Steganography—surpassing all others—not without great and continuous labor, with the help of God, the Best and Greatest and forever blessed. Lest, clearly, it happens that those working through them err in the order, names, characters, powers, or knowledge, we have deemed it necessary to arrange a general table of all of them and a summary for the memory in this chapter. This table, so that it may be seen on a single page, contains the 31 principal Spirits, each of whom presides in his own office and order over all the operations of our steganography about which we have spoken in this first book, assigning to each one his appropriated character <note>original: "charactere" — sigil</note>, number, and order of Princes, Dukes, Counts, servants, and sub-servants in their proper ranks. We are joining this table so that those who desire to study in this art might observe the diversity of operations without error. For indeed, the great mysteries of this art cannot be penetrated except by the most studious men. And even by those, only if the love of knowledge and humility move them to excel. First, they must be warned to keep the art itself hidden <note>original: "occultam" — A central theme in Renaissance esotericism: knowledge must be kept from the "unworthy" to prevent its misuse.</note>, lest it fall into the hands and knowledge of the wicked, who might commit many execrable crimes through it. For even if the art itself is truly good in its essence, its practice <note>original: "practica"</note> would nevertheless lead no less to evil and the wicked than to the good and the virtuous. Therefore, let what would be harmful if published among the wicked remain secret among the good. For unless the spirit sees that character of his superior, he will treat the one calling him with injury or otherwise completely despise him. We send letters, however, for a twofold reason, although we can announce a secret through the spirit alone: both so that we may free men from suspicion by the written character, and so that we may more tightly bind the spirit, obligated by that very character, to obedience.

# BOOK TWO

In the preceding book, with the help of the most high GOD, I arranged 31 ranks of Spirits—the supreme Commanders <term>Imperatores | In this system, 'Commanders' represent the primary keys or spirits governing a specific section of the work</term> of our art—along with two Companions <term>Comitibus | Assistants or secondary keys</term> and their servants necessary for our operation, which we have organized with no small labor. Although their services are sufficient for the administration of all secrets (no matter how hidden they may be) for every practitioner, we wished to join this second book to the first lest we seem to omit anything that might contribute to the perfection of the art. 

Since, however, for each hour of the day and night, specific spirits are assigned—by the tradition of certain wise men—to various operations, divine tasks, and wonderful effects, it pleased us to follow their order, though without superstition. We seek only to obtain from them what serves our purpose without harming the Christian name. But the rest, being vain things full of superstitions and contrary to our faith, let us pass over. Therefore, for each hour of both the day and the night, we shall track down the appointed spirits and the selection of Solomon, surnamed Hermes <note>A reference to the 'Testament of Solomon' or the 'Hermetic' tradition, common sources for Renaissance magic and cryptography</note>, in his volume on magic. These are the principal Spirits, acting as the supreme Commanders <term>Imperatores</term> of the art, along with the other officials necessary for our proposed operation, whom we will pursue in abundance. 

We shall give both the method and instruction to all students of this art, so that they might reveal the foreknown spirits by a more skillful counsel to the Companions <term>Comitibus</term> of their months, on certain days, and at every hour. For each prince presides freely over his Spirits, Companions, and servants like a Commander <term>Imperator</term>; they come to him whenever they are called by us with the lawful Chant <term>Carmine | A ritualized poem or incantation used to trigger the cryptographic process</term>, bringing forth the secrets entrusted to them, and showing themselves obedient and ready for us in all things.

<margin>
But since regarding the manner and position of the Spirits...
</margin>

I should demonstrate once more, that you may know I must declare again: nothing in this art is considered frivolous, nothing is superstitious, and nothing is contrary to Evangelical doctrine. For all things which we have either said in the preceding book, or will say in those following, are supported by lawful and honest principles and by only the very best instructions. For just as mystery and words are wrapped in names, they require a learned reader. Indeed, we use the service of spirits for a veiled meaning <note>Trithemius uses the language of "spirits" as a metaphor for cryptographic keys; the "veiled meaning" is the encrypted message itself</note>, which he knows is made public to the wicked. And lest anyone fail through error in the calculation of the hours, let them know that we have increased the planetary hours <term>horas planetarum | Unlike fixed sixty-minute hours, planetary hours divide the period from sunrise to sunset into twelve equal parts, meaning their length changes with the seasons</term> both in the day and in the night.

->CHAPTER ONE<-

Samael is the principal and supreme Commander <term>Imperator | In this system, the primary key or presiding entity for a specific timeframe</term> who presides over the first hour of the day. And he has under his command many Dukes and Counts, whom he sends in this hour alone when called by a practitioner skilled in Steganography <term>Steganographia | From the Greek 'steganos' (hidden) and 'graphein' (to write); the art of secret communication</term>. Now, the first hour of the day is to be calculated from sunrise and according to the planetary system. The aforementioned spirits carry out the secret communication of matters; but if they are called outside of their specific hour, they utterly disdain to come. 

And note that the dukes and princes of Samael are rarely sent by him for the service of the steganocenter <term>steganocentri | Likely referring to the central operations or the "core" of the cryptographic system</term>, for they perform their duty in attending to the great and nightly illusions of men. (However, they and their successors are specially deputed for the service of the steganographic art, which cannot happen without divine permission. For they themselves are from the supreme order among the spirits, and show themselves somewhat proud and rebellious to those calling them; nor do they easily obey anyone except the most skilled in the art without labor and danger. For they are arrogant and most ready for illusions and mockery; they laugh at and sneer especially at those whom they find less skilled in the Steganographic art. But those whom they find bold, steadfast, and expert in the art itself, they revere and fear, and they always obey their commands most promptly with trembling and obedience.)

# CHAPTER XXIV

The hour of this spirit is called <term>Sephar</term> <note>Likely a derived Hebrew name, possibly related to "Sepher" (book/writing) or "Sapphire."</note>, and its superior Angel is **Samadiel**. # CHAPTER XXV

Whoever desires to approach the understanding of this our occult art, and through it longs to perform wonders, it is first necessary that he be adorned with **Virtues**, and a clean conscience, with good will toward God and neighbor. In no way should he be prone to harming anyone, nor should he seek the dealings of superstition. Next, it is necessary that he be most thoroughly steeped in the good arts and the knowledge of human letters, and especially well-versed in the <term>science of the stars</term> <note>In the 15th century, "scientia astrorum" encompassed both what we now call astronomy and astrology.</note>. For we believe it is possible for only a few—and even among the most learned, hardly any—to come to this science without a teacher. It is necessary, moreover, that the teacher be not only proven and experienced in the knowledge of things, but also faithful, pious, and God-fearing. For the purer the science is toward God, the more successful and secure he will be in the operation of this science, for the **Spirits** and **Virtues** obey [such a person]. # BOOK III OF JOHANNES TRITEMIUS'S
# STEGANOGRAPHY

After we have completed the first two books of our art with God’s help—in which it was necessary to describe both types of steganography—we now add this third volume to them. Here, by adding marvelous things, we shall connect things even more invisible. I read in a certain ancient book by a philosopher of the Indians, who taught and demonstrated that it is possible through a specific art to make the thoughts of our mind known to a friend, no matter how far away they may be, within twenty-four hours—without words, without letters, and without a messenger, in a manner most perfect, expansive, and secret. Driven by a most intense desire for knowledge, I began to wish to test this for myself, or rather to find the truth of it. After many labors, I finally discovered the science itself, proven through experience. 

This is now the greatest secret of the art, and it is shrouded in such obscurities that it is easily accessible to no one. For Menastor <note>Menastor is a figure Trithemius identifies as a source of secret knowledge, possibly a corruption of a historical or mythical name.</note> withheld it as a mystery from all but a very few. And so that this secret might remain so powerful, it seems that until now I have been unable to find anyone who has dared to make it clearer through any speech or written record. 

However, I feared that such excellent works might—due to their extreme obscurity—either be held in contempt by the unlearned or eventually be burned. Since I have already proven the art in many trials, I wished to record it in more stellar <note>original: *astrioribus literis*. This suggests a form of writing or encoding related to celestial or higher intellectual matters.</note> letters. I have done this so that, with God’s help, it might be of some use to learned men and those devoted to great studies, while remaining forever hidden from these unlearned salt-eaters <term>salt-eaters: translated from the Greek *haliophagos*. Trithemius uses this term to disparage the "common" or "crude" people who consume only the physical 'salt' of knowledge without understanding its spiritual essence.</term>, and in no way understandable to their dull intellects.

<summary>Trithemius introduces the third book of his work, claiming to have discovered an ancient Indian method for transmitting thoughts across vast distances without physical messages. He explains his decision to document this secret in a sophisticated way to protect it from the "unlearned" while making it available to scholars.</summary>

**T**he Monk said: There are seven planets over which seven angels preside. Subject to these are twenty-one spirits—specifically three for each angel—through whom they reveal hidden secrets; their names are set forth in the preceding table. These are the seven angels of the planets according to the tradition of the ancient sages. <margin># The Angel of the Moon</margin>
<margin>☉ <note>Symbol for the Sun</note></margin>

After him came Anael of Venus <note>♀</note>, then the angel of Jupiter <note>♃</note>, after him that of Mercury <note>☿</note>, then Mars <note>♂</note>, next the Moon <note>☽</note>, and finally the Sun <note>☉</note>—each for 354 years and 4 months. It is believed that each angel in the table provided above was assigned a specific number as their lordly domain. Thus, the wise believe that at the time of the Great Flood, Samael, the angel of Mars, held dominion; but Gabriel held it at the time of the confusion of languages <note>The biblical event of the Tower of Babel</note>. Michael, the angel of the Sun, held it at the time of Israel's exodus from Egypt. Finally, if anyone places faith in the aforementioned claim, he himself will easily be able to calculate the changes of the ages and the stewardships of the angels from the beginning of the world down to his own time, following the prescribed order.

We, however, in pursuing those things which lead to our purpose, do not admit any other spirits subject to the seven planetary angels except for the twenty-one mentioned before, through which we work the effect of our instruction by the "fires of our intention" <note>original: "per ignes intentionis nostræ"; this likely refers to the mental focus or the cryptographic "spark" required to activate the system.</note>. We shall observe the customary order of the planets, beginning from Saturn, the highest of all, and descending to the Moon. We will show the primary operation to be maintained under each angel, and then we will join the chapters of those spirits serving him in their proper order.

# CHAPTER ONE
->Concerning the first and highest<-
->Angel of Saturn, Orifiel,<-
->and the operations<-
->which are performed through him<-

Saturn is the highest and supreme of all the planets, slow in motion and cold in nature, because it is far removed from the earth. From the point of its beginning, it completes its circuit in thirty years to the point of its first station. It remains in each sign of the zodiac for thirty months; in its nearly natural motion, it travels for six months and twenty-eight days. Its first and highest Angel, according to the opinion of the ancients, is called Orifiel. He has other principal Spirits under him—namely Cadach, Domiel, and Morofiel—about whom we shall speak in their proper place. Through this great Orifiel, the Angel of Saturn, many and diverse operations are performed in <term>Steganography</term> <note>Literally "hidden writing." Trithemius uses this term to describe a system of secret communication that he presents through the metaphor of angelic magic.</note>. For through him, we can make our minds, our concepts, and our intentions known to a friend <note>original: "mentes nostras conceptum ac animum nostrum facere amico hunc autem sciendi"</note> wherever they may be, by letters if it is pleasing, or even without letters. And many other marvelous things may be performed, which no one understands except for one who is skilled in this science.

Therefore, if anyone wishes to perform any work in Steganography through this Angel, especially on the day of Saturn <note>Saturday</note>, it is necessary to know briefly about those things subject to Saturn, so that he may know its diverse and varied motions—namely: primary, proper, mixed, direct, retrograde, and stationary. And in all these things, it is necessary to know not only the general rules handed down by Astronomers <note>In the 15th century, the distinction between "astronomer" and "astrologer" was not yet fixed; here it refers to those who calculate the positions and influences of celestial bodies.</note> (for although they are greatly conducive to this science, they are not entirely sufficient), but it is also necessary to know the specific details.

Therefore, as a foundation, after frequently setting out the tables and rules concerning the motions of the planets—which are absolutely necessary for any practitioner in this art—we shall add special rules and tables of particular motions throughout the individual chapters <gloss>of this book</gloss>. Without the observation of these rules, no one can operate in the said art.

And note well that the day of any planet is divided into four equal parts. The first of these, consisting of the first three <term>unequal hours</term> <note>Unlike standard 60-minute hours, "unequal" or "planetary" hours are calculated by dividing the period from sunrise to sunset into 12 equal parts. Depending on the season, these hours can be much longer or shorter than 60 minutes.</note> counted from sunrise, is governed by the principal Angel of that planet. The three remaining quarters of the <term>artificial day</term> <note>The "artificial day" refers to the time from sunrise to sunset, as opposed to the "natural day" of 24 hours.</note> are governed in order by the three substitute Angels of the said principal Angel.

->For example.<-

On the day of Saturn <note>Saturday</note>, Orifiel—the first and principal Angel of said day—possesses for himself the first three unequal planetary hours calculated from sunrise. The first Angel among the substitutes of Orifiel, who is called Sadael, holds the second three hours. Somiel, who is otherwise second in the order of Orifiel's substitutes, holds the third three. And the third and last of the substitutes, called Marafiel, holds the fourth or last three.

During the first hours of the day of Saturn <note>original symbol: ♄</note>, one must work through Orifiel in matters subject to Saturn; during the second [hours] through Sadael; during the third through Somiel, and so on. All operations, whether for good or <unclear>otherwise</unclear>, will obtain a <unclear>prosperous</unclear> or weak effect <note>Trithemius suggests that timing is critical: if the work is performed during the wrong angel's hour, the magical or cryptographic transmission will fail or be weakened.</note>. In the same way, on the remaining days, one must work during the four parts of the day through the specific angels assigned to them.

# On the Various Motion of the Planets and the Interpretation of the Tables

##

Although in the present chapter we are specifically to hold a discussion regarding the motions of Saturn $\hbar$ and its spirits, as well as the operations of <term>steganography<gloss>The art of hidden writing; here used in a magical or astrological context to encode messages through planetary symbols.</gloss></term> through the heart <note>original: "p. cor." Likely an abbreviation for "per corda" (through the hearts), a specific method mentioned in the works of Johannes Trithemius.</note>, the studious reader should be advised to remember what we say in this chapter for the following ones, lest we be forced to repeat what is aptly stated in every single chapter. For there are various motions of the individual planets, and they are divided very finely into various others; yet to us, the motion is more specifically multiple and varies with many most subtle divisions. Whether it be **direct**, **retrograde**, or **mixed**, etc., it is defined by almost as many varying points as are marked out from the beginning of its motion in the circle <note>The "circle" refers to the planet's orbit or its path through the zodiac.</note>. What shall I say of the combination of these planets with one another? For if, as Ptolemy says in his *Centiloquium* <note>original: "Centiloquio." A famous collection of 100 astrological aphorisms traditionally attributed to the astronomer Claudius Ptolemy.</note>, there are 120 combinations among the planets themselves: namely, 21 pairings, 35 groups of three, 35 groups of four, 21 groups of five, 7 groups of six, and one group of seven. We shall speak of these in their proper place.

Regarding the other motions, although we cannot give a certain limit because of the infinite diversity with which they vary daily—through the aforementioned <term>ascensions<gloss>The rising of a zodiacal sign or planet above the horizon.</gloss></term> or calculations—being fully unknown to the uninitiated, nevertheless, as far as we have been able to observe, we have found more than 30,000 divisions in which all the operations of the art often vary in their effect. And unless one is very expert in all these things, and knows the <term>mean motions<gloss>The average, uniform speed of a planet, used as a baseline for calculating its actual, variable position.</gloss></term> of all the planets perfectly, and then the most minute point-divisions—which arise from fourths, thirds, seconds, minutes, and degrees, and even more subtly divided than those—he will easily fall into various errors and will hardly escape into the grace of knowing.

# On the Various Motion of the Planets and the Interpretation of the Tables

##

Therefore, this instruction in the science being perfected, we have arranged three tables. In the first of these, we have placed the motion of **Saturn** according to the four parts of both day and night, so that we have reduced the <term>root<gloss>The "radix" or starting point in astronomical calculations, often the position of a planet at a specific significant moment in time.</gloss></term> to the specific point. We have also arranged the point of the **true ascendant** for any given sign, starting from the first degree of the east; having set forth 641 by 8 and 700 <note>The significance of these specific numbers—641, 8, and 700—is unclear, but they likely refer to specific chronological epochs or calculation constants used by the author.</note>, we have written down the entire **Zodiac** in the second table.

Finally, in the same second table, we have distributed the motion of **Saturn** in each of the twelve signs to all the quarters of the day and night down to the **minutes** <note>original: "minutias." In an astronomical context, this refers to the 60 minutes that make up one degree of the zodiac.</note>, so that at any hour of the night, once the degree of the ascendant is known in which Saturn itself resides, its principal root can clearly be made manifest. However, once this divine calculation is finished—which I know not if our age <note>The author often uses "our age" to refer to the current human lifespan or the present era of history.</note> can fully attain—the table must be started anew from the beginning of its principle.

In the third table, which is **sevenfold**, we have reduced the **Conjunction of Saturn** with the other planets to the proportion of the point—since this conjunction is unique—through which all the others, from the **Sun**, etc., are easily reduced to the point.

In the same table, we have placed the primary motion of all the planets through the aforesaid division of every beginning, progression, and elongation from the point in any motion separately, provided that the **mean motion** <term>mean motion<gloss>The average speed at which a planet travels in its orbit, assuming a perfectly circular path, used as a baseline for more complex calculations.</gloss></term> is first perfectly grasped. For without knowledge of the mean motion, it is impossible for anyone to attain this practical wisdom with authority. Furthermore, even if you understand the mean and **true motion** <term>true motion<gloss>The actual position and speed of a planet as observed from Earth, which varies due to the elliptical nature of orbits.</gloss></term> perfectly, it will profit you nothing in the knowledge of this science unless you understand the three prescribed tables in their entirety, according to every point of division in the planetary motions, taken equally from unequal degrees, down to each individual minute. But now let us proceed to the operations.

### and is called Orifiel; he observes the
### governance of the first quarter.

The first and principal Angel of ♄ <note>Saturn</note>, as we have said in the preceding pages, is **Orifiel**. Along with the other angels of the planets, he governs the world in his proper order for **354 years and 4 months**. He holds the **first quarter** <note>Medieval timekeeping often divided the day and night into four equal quarters to determine which spiritual influence was strongest</note> both in the day and in the night. Through him, the operation is carried out from the rising of the ☉ <note>Sun</note> in the day, and from its setting at night, up to the third hour inclusive, in all matters that pertain to Saturn, and on Saturn's day and night. 

Therefore, when you wish to announce something to an absent person during the first quarter of ♄ <note>Saturn</note>—without spoken words and without written letters—through the spirit of ♄, no one other than **Orifiel** must be called by you, as through him you will be able to announce all things most perfectly.

Let us complete the degrees of ♄ <note>Saturn</note> in the sign of ♉ <note>Taurus</note>, and it will be 30. Let us then multiply 30 by 25, and they produce 750. # PICATRIX

Alphonso, King of Spain <note>Alphonso X "the Wise" of Castile (reigned 1252–1284), a famed patron of science and translation</note>, and of all Andalusia, commanded that this book be translated with the greatest zeal and the highest diligence from the Arabic into the Spanish language, to the praise and glory of the Most High and Almighty God, whose nature it is to reveal the secrets of the sciences to those he has predestined, and also for the enlightenment of the Latin scholars, who suffer from a scarcity of books published by the ancient Philosophers.

It was compiled from 224 Books of Philosophy, and this most wise Philosopher called it by its own name, the **Spanish Picatrix** <note>original: "Picatrix Hispaniensis"</note>. It was completed in the Year 1256 of the Lord; 1295 of Caesar <note>The "Era of Caesar" or Spanish Era, a calendar commonly used in the Iberian Peninsula where year 1 begins in 38 BCE</note>; 1568 of Alexander <note>The Seleucid Era, used frequently in the Near East, beginning in 312 BCE</note>; and 655 of the Arabs <note>The Hijri (Islamic) calendar</note>.

->This work is dedicated only to the wise.<-

# BOOK I
## Concerning the science of knowing, and at what level it stands.
### Chapter 1.

Know, O dearest brother: that the greatest and most noble gift which GOD has given to the people of this world is KNOWLEDGE <note>original: *scire*. In this context, it refers to both the act of knowing and the body of knowledge itself.</note>, because through knowledge one gains awareness of ancient things, which are the souls of all things of this world, and which causes are more closely related to the causes of other things, and how one thing has agreement with another, and why all things that exist are as they are, and how one thing is raised after another in order, and in what place He exists, who is the root and principle of the things of this world, and through Him all things are dissolved, and through Him all things new and old are known. For He is in Truth the first, and nothing is lacking in Him, nor does He need anything else, since He Himself is the first and is the cause of other things, nor does He receive qualities from another. He is not a body, nor composed of any body, nor is He <gloss>except</gloss> mixed with any other thing outside Himself, but is entirely in Himself. And therefore He cannot be called "One" <note>The author is navigating a complex theological point: God is so uniquely "One" that the human word for the number one barely applies.</note> except that He is properly One Truth and One Unity, and through His Unity every single thing has unity. And He Himself is the first Truth, nor does He need any other Truth. For every single thing receives Truth from Him; all things without Him

# The First Book

## Chapter 1.

As an introduction, it is essential to understand that there are two creatures within Man. The precious [divine] one and the other. The divine is created out of Adam through God the Father; the [new] one is created through God the Son, in every person who believes in Him. Now, whatever dies in the creature of God the Father does not rise again to Eternal Life; but that which dies in God the Son does. Therefore, the whole essence of this matter is to correctly recognize these two creatures. These creatures are without [physical] substance and without material essence. Within themselves, they are enclosed so that no separate body is divided from them.

Now, our old Adam is his body, namely the creation of God the Father; and the creation of God the Son is joined to it. And just as all works of the Father are visible—the Earth and all things—so the Son serves invisibly, and yet on both sides it is the same body, one form, in every shape within the light of God.

Therefore, the basis of the Lord’s Supper <note>original: "Cena Domini"</note> is to correctly recognize these two mentioned bodies and their distinction. And just as Father and Son are equal to one another, so we too see the Father, and yet there is one Father; and we see the Son, and yet there is one God. In this way, we make known the various works; they remain in their form, but are not one body. God the Son does not create his creature differently than the Father, but rather He renews it—that is, He makes another equal to it, and formed nothing new. For the old form remains standing in Heaven.

## CHAPTER IV.

-> --- <-

The unchanging body exists in this invisible state just like the soul. It possesses the nature and essence of the soul and is always endowed with its qualities. For this reason, it can pass through other objects, just as the body of Christ passed through locked doors. The soul unites with it, and while the soul itself does not possess a physical nature (but rather the opposite), both nonetheless share a human nature. 

Therefore, this body gravitates toward the one in whose image it was made—namely, Christ. There alone will it be nourished, and not here on Earth. Consequently, we must not try to perceive or understand this body as having any infirmity or illness. Instead, we should always regard it as being like the body of Christ, which passed through locked doors and rose from the sealed tomb through the specific power of God. Thus, the **glorified body** is no longer subject to death.

# CHAPTER V

Every creature rejoices in its origin <note>original: "uhrsprungs," meaning source or beginning</note>: the angels eat angels' bread <note>a reference to Manna or divine nourishment</note>; man eats the bread of the earth; the Holy Trinity feeds upon itself. This **New Body** is conceived in Baptism. Because we are currently physically mortal, we cannot naturally understand this spiritual corporeality. Nevertheless, it is so: just as no body can exist without food, God wills that the earthly body be fed by the earth. Likewise, this New Body comes from Christ through the commandment of the **Lord's Supper**. 

Because we are alienated <note>referring to the state of fallen man</note> and hunger to receive according to the old body, we instead receive for the New Body. We do not eat according to [the old way], but according to the commandment of **Remembrance**—the Remembrance of the New Body of Christ on the Cross, His suffering, and His New Blood shed upon the Cross.

# The Second Book
## From John the Evangelist

John chapter 6 is to be held in particularly high regard among us as an explainer or interpreter of the other Evangelists <note>The "other Evangelists" refers to Matthew, Mark, and Luke, known as the Synoptic Gospels</note>. Especially regarding what the other three reported about the sacramental power of the Supper—John explains all of this better and more extensively than the others. For he takes the explanation solely from the mouth of God, although he speaks somewhat more hiddenly or obscurely. Even though the clear Evangelists agree that it is God's word, and nothing depends on the flesh or a foreign sense [of the text], we must therefore perceive their understanding or the word of God through the Holy Spirit, not through the dead letters. And the sum of John's message is that holiness must have its beginning here on Earth. Whoever does not attain salvation <term>Seeligkeit: Archaic spelling of *Seligkeit*, meaning blessedness or the state of being saved</term> here on Earth will find nothing more after their death. Therefore, the saints on Earth must likewise have their food of holiness here on Earth just as in heaven in the kingdom of the Father <note>original Latin: *regno patris*</note>; and it is one food, for there is one community of the saints in heaven and on Earth, and not two different kinds. Therefore, a "help" was spoken of by Christ: for His will is in heaven as it is on Earth. Accordingly, whoever does not eat from the table of Christ here on Earth is also deprived of it there in heaven. Therefore, John stands upon this foundation, namely in the interpretation of the power of this food as eternal life <note>original Latin: *Vita eterna*</note>, not in the consumption of the flesh <note>original Latin: *carnis*</note>. For he says:

->“Work for the food that remains”<-
<note>original Latin: *Operamini Cibum qui manet*. This is a reference to John 6:27, where Jesus encourages his followers to seek spiritual nourishment over physical food.</note>

By this, it is well understood that this food is no filling of the belly, but rather an imperishable and remaining food of our eternal life; for the eternal is found therein, which

->“the Son of Man will give”<-
<note>original Latin: *Quem filius hominis dabit*</note>

That is Christ, the Son of Man: therefore He gives us the food to eat bodily as a Man, not as a spirit or a shadow; but yet it is spiritual, heavenly, indestructible food, which Death cannot consume or overcome for all eternity.

<meta>This page transitions from the specific examination of the Gospel of John to a broader interpretation of various sayings across all four Gospels, specifically focusing on the theological nature of "bread" and the conflict between spiritual truth and human reason as it relates to the Lord's Supper.</meta>

# The Third Book
## An explanation of several sayings across the four Evangelists pertaining to the Supper.

Because the text of the Evangelists is itself, in a belittling way, cast aside by human reason, it is no wonder that these sayings are so strangely changed by them. For in the main matter or central point, many write of delightful sayings which are not the primary Articles of Faith; this happens because they set human reason above the statutes of God. Nevertheless, Christ did not only have humans as adversaries, but also the Devil; and our Lord God set Him against those who opposed Christ. And the spirits have a greater understanding than men; but when men unite themselves with such spirits and devils, that is their great unbelief and they commit a great despair of damnation by allowing themselves to be drawn in. Therefore, Christ encountered many things, about which he had to make himself known and heard in various ways through words—words which might be interpreted against Christ then and thereafter.

Thus, the Devil <note>original: *Diabolus*</note> also tempted Christ and demanded much of him, saying: *Make it so these stones become bread* <note>original Latin: *fac ut lapides panis*; see Matthew 4:3</note>. This was not because he wanted to eat them, but rather so that a sense of pride might enter Him. Those of his kind treat him in the same way.

Man lives by two breads: the earthly Adamite bread and the Heavenly bread. The Heavenly bread is the Word of God, the Flesh of the Divine <note>original Latin: *Caro Di[vini]*</note>: namely the word of God that comes out of the mouth of God. The Flesh of the Word <note>original Latin: *Caro [verbi]*</note>: the word that has become flesh in JESUS CHRIST. That is: man shall consist of two kinds of bread; that is, not the eternal man alone—namely the Adamite or old Jewish man—but the New Man in addition. And a king; and two breads. And a man also takes hold of this.

The Devil did not understand such a word of Christ. Christ answered the Devil humanly according to his demand and question, but not from the Devil’s heart. For he had desired to bite into the Heavenly word in his heart, and questioned the Lord.

Now, the "flesh of the bread" <note>original Latin: *Caro panis*</note> will not be useful on its own, but rather the "Flesh of the Word" <note>original Latin: *Caro verbi*</note> in the resurrection <note>original Latin: *in resurrectione*</note>. For the flesh of Adam is in itself, quite alone, of no use, because it is without spirit.

It specifically contrasts the "earthly bread" of Adam with the "Heavenly bread" of Christ's fleshly Word, a distinction vital for understanding the Eucharist and the Resurrection.</summary>

## You are those who have stayed with me <note>original Latin: *Vos estis qui permansistis mecum*; see Luke 22:28.</note>

Indeed, Christ has the power to insist that He does not want the learned ones to maintain His Kingdom through their disputations. Instead, He wants the poor and the suffering, who do not receive His word with a full belly <note>This is a metaphor for those who are spiritually complacent or satisfied with worldly wealth.</note>, but remain in humility and misery from the beginning to the end. Therefore, God's table provides no joy to those who are "full." For God's table is not given to everyone. One person is deprived of the table through false order; another through false usage; a third does not see it at all. A fourth eats of it to their damnation. Therefore, one must pay close attention to whom God makes a partaker of His table: namely, the poor and the suffering. 

If we now wish to enjoy the table of Christ's Father in Heaven, we must first seek and possess the Kingdom of His Son here on Earth, so that we may be invited just as we wish to be in Heaven. Christ's Kingdom is on Earth; the Father's Kingdom is in heaven; and it is one and the same food in both places. Therefore, we pray daily for both Kingdoms in the "Our Father": and we desire both toward heaven and on Earth. Therefore, Luke and the other Evangelists powerfully confirm the Last Supper through the parable of the table in the Kingdom of the Father, showing that one table provides both one food and one drink.

### Upon the Thrones <note>original Latin: *Super Thronos*; see Luke 22:30.</note>

In heaven, there is no earthly part. God is not carried by His angels. However, the Apostles and saints will have heavenly seats <note>The author uses the word *stüle* (stools/chairs), referring to the thrones of judgment mentioned in the Gospels.</note> upon which they shall judge. They will not be carried by angels; it will not be in spirit [only], but in flesh and body; each person shall sit in a human manner and a heavenly nature. # The Fourth Book from St. Paul

If there were a different essence to the Lord's Supper <note>term: *Nachtmal*; the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note> than what the Evangelists set forth, then Paul would not have described it. But he lets it remain with the Evangelists, without any figures or tropes <note>figures of speech or metaphors</note>, so that it remains truly eating and drinking, yet naturally. What the Father’s person spoke through, the other body cannot [contradict]. Otherwise, one goes forth. Therefore it remains and increases.

Paul is the Interpreter or Hermeneut <note>original: *Hermene.*; one who explains or interprets sacred texts.</note> of Christ. And upon him all our discord is founded, especially in the controversy over the Lord's Supper; all doubt is settled by [his] decision.

<margin>Paul</margin>
Because Paul leaves a human body in the Lord's Supper—which humans can understand simply, as our language allows—we should also leave it at that. We should not seek some "angelic" or supernatural understanding, nor make spiritual what Christ intended to be bodily. And also on our side, in the eating and drinking of the body and blood of Christ, we should grasp it as the words sound. But how it happens, we cannot grasp with our reason. Because it is ungraspable, we must be taught from above and be born again: we cannot grasp this in any other way than through faith and trust in Christ—that it is as He said—even though our eyes see only a body. And that is the power of the words of his Supper. For we cannot grasp with our best [intellect] how it is, so that his heartfelt humanity is one with those who eat; and [it brings] peace to our Spirit.

How much less [can we grasp] what Christ gives us in bread and wine. For our eyes see nothing but false things <note>The author suggests that our physical senses are easily deceived by the mere appearance of bread and wine, failing to see the spiritual reality.</note>. Therefore, we must still comply with nature according to God's command, which is: we want to receive the Lord Christ's body through eating and drinking, God granting how far or how much it flows bodily into us and remains or not. So, although we receive the flesh and blood of Christ through our stomach, we desire the spiritual life. Therefore, how much more must we believe and trust Christ, since we trust his Father. Therefore it is commanded to man alone in both creatures <note>term: *Kreaturn*; here referring to the "created elements" of bread and wine.</note>, wine and bread, for the Spirit. In this way, the human must still enjoy and understand through the act of drinking. For from Paul it is his sign, that the Word of God and his body are not two bodies, but one. <margin>1 Corinthians 11</margin>
# WHEN YOU COME TOGETHER
<note>original Latin: *Cum Convenitis*; a reference to 1 Corinthians 11:20</note>
