For the spiritual longing and devotion of the soul, in which the Lord's Supper of Christ is established, defines the "days" of the Corinthians.

The Last Supper was not merely a "Supper of the Lord" <note>original Latin: *Coena Domini*</note>. For the order of the Supper dictates that Christ first ate the <unclear>Passover</unclear> <note>original German: *Passhal*; the Jewish Passover meal</note>, and only afterward distributed the Sacrament. Therefore, no one should indulge in filling their own bellies or in <unclear>crudeness</unclear>; rather, they should have a common meal in the memory of the meal <margin>of His body</margin>. The bread "broke" Him, for it was a breaking of His body, not just the breaking of bread; nor is it enough to be merely "devout" toward the physical body, but rather what is held in the hand serves as a sign so that all may become partakers of His body. Without this "breaking" <note>the crucifixion</note>, salvation could not have been possible or come to pass. For where this is not present in the sacrifice, one does not truly receive that body and blood or share in His suffering.

Those who seize spiritual goods for themselves follow in the "footsteps of Judas" <note>original Latin: *in Vestigio Judas*</note> with the money-bag. These people and their like partake of the Supper unworthily. He who does not rightly distinguish his own body—whether it be physical or not—also fails to distinguish it from the body of the Lord. The "weak" are those who reflect on their sins but refuse to abandon them for the sake of self-interest.
The "sleeping," however, are those who take no conscience of what is good, but consume themselves unto <unclear>death</unclear> without any remorse for their sins. When the Supper is not received rightly, one enters into a bad conscience. Sin must be distinguished, for the Word wishes to prepare us against evil. Therefore, let us examine ourselves. Each of us is responsible for himself. Therefore, <unclear>Paul</unclear> speaks these strong words of God, which were interpreted according to the words of the Evangelist John <margin>for John and other redeemed ones</margin>. And not the other way around <note>original Latin: *Et non econtra*</note>.

<meta>This page continues the theological discussion of the Lord's Supper, moving from the practical instructions in 1 Corinthians to a deeper investigation of how the Old Testament prophets provide the necessary foundation for understanding the "New Creation" and the relationship between the physical and spiritual elements of the Sacrament.</meta>

# The Fifth Book from the
# Prophecy of the Prophets

As was initially stated, all points and articles of the Christian faith, as they are contained in the Gospel, cannot be thoroughly recognized or understood except through the writings of the prophets; therefore, as far as the prophets indicate, we should <term>affirm<note>original German: *astruieren*; from the Latin *astruere*, meaning to build upon, support, or prove an argument.</note></term> our faith, etc.

Now, the Lord’s Supper <note>original German: *Nachtmal*</note> is the highest article of all others regarding faith in Christ; therefore, we ought to diligently look through the prophets so that we do not go astray in this article. For here lies the <term>New Creature<note>A reference to "New Creation" from 2 Corinthians 5:17, signifying the transformative effect of Christ’s work on the believer.</note></term>, in which all laws are fulfilled. Therefore, we must believe everything that Christ says—that it is so—and combined with that faith, enjoy a simple eating and drinking, lovely to consume, which the teeth cannot grasp <note>This suggests that while the mouth physically eats, the true essence of the Sacrament is spiritual and cannot be "chewed" or understood by physical means alone.</note>.

Now, two kinds of eating have been thought of: a physical one and a spiritual one. And either one may be believed. However, it is not to be taken that way. For Christ did not separate the Body and the Spirit from one another. Therefore, one cannot eat spiritually here unless it is also physical, and vice versa.

In the Lord's Supper, one cannot eat only spiritually, for the Spirit that previously "hovered over the water" <note>A reference to the Creation account in Genesis 1:2.</note> or flew, became flesh in the Virgin Mary. Thus, Spirit and flesh are one thing, and vice versa. Therefore, whoever wishes to have one must also have the other. For our part, the bare flesh is of no use, but the spiritual, which is God, united with the flesh, is useful. And if Christ’s flesh is to be rightly named, it is a spiritual flesh, or a spiritualized flesh; that is to say, it is called "spiritualized" because it is conceived of the Spirit and not from the human, which is a sinful and worldly flesh.

Paul says: <note>Refers to 2 Corinthians 3:6</note> "The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life" <note>original Latin: *littera occidit, spiritus autem vivificat*</note>. The letter is of the letter, therefore it is <term>death-dealing<note>original German: *todwirge*; literally "death-strangling" or "deadly."</note></term>; but Spirit is of the Spirit, and is God Himself. So, if the letter is not God's word, it must be of use; therefore, the letter must be God’s. For this reason, Christ’s flesh did not grow from the earth, even though it was truly flesh and looked almost identical to other flesh that comes from the earth.

The prophets and their interpretations were also written out of the Holy Spirit, just like the old Adam; thus, consider those who belong to the New Adam, to whom the command of God through Christ distributed everything. The word of Christ was prophesied. Likewise, his <term>forerunner<note>Likely referring to John the Baptist or the prophets who preceded Christ.</note></term> preached the word of God according to his understanding through the Holy Spirit. For they—the prophets—entrusted the power of interpretation to God, having received everything from God. Therefore, he who does not have the prophets within him regarding the entire sum of the holy Gospels does not understand the proclamation. For such people only create sects, <unclear>desecrate</unclear> the temple of God, and <unclear>betray</unclear> the universal Church of God. For they are not born from God from above.

The Father is also Christ’s Son: that is the faith and love of Peter; we then, as stones, are built upon Him into a temple because we have been released from all external things. <note>A reference to 1 Peter 2:5, where believers are described as "living stones" being built into a spiritual house.</note>

The fact that for Moses, water was transformed into blood, meant nothing other than the transformation of wine into the blood of Christ; this is so that He may become an essential and true blood within us. And just as Pharaoh and his people drowned in the Red or bloody Sea, so too in the New Testament are those who partake of the blood of Christ unworthily and have no true faith in this article of the Last Supper.

The <term>Paschal Lamb</term> <note>original Latin: *Agnus paschalis*</note> is not the body of Christ in the same way it was taught in the Old Testament, which prefigured it in the wine; thus, in the New Testament, whoever eats of it unworthily shall be rooted out from Israel. Those who have now followed God in His order and have eaten the Passover Lamb have been redeemed through <unclear>Jesus</unclear> <note>OCR: *Isum*; likely a shorthand or scribal error for *Iesum* (Jesus).</note>. For they have eaten the Last Supper of Christ in the Spirit. This is the remembrance of the Supper, held one after another until the coming of Christ, just as they held the true Supper early on and have it until the Last Day. And just as the figurative, physical elements of the Old Testament signified the physical presence in the New Testament, so we must also enjoy Christ physically; for He also did nothing un-physically and was no ghost, but a man. Therefore, His Supper must be understood physically. And just as He hated those who were disobedient to His Father in the Old Testament and did not eat the Passover Lamb worthily, so His Father hates the stumblers who do not believe in His Son.

You will find a further explanation in my great exposition of the Old Testament, from line to line. Therefore, we should seek no further sacrifice in the Last Supper, for we have nothing to sacrifice but our own—only our body and life, according to the word of God. And what we lose in this way will be given back to us, for God keeps nothing of that which we sacrifice to Him; He gives it back to us and even more besides. Therefore, bread and wine, silver and gold, are not our own property; rather, they belong to us and our neighbor. And we have nothing to hand over to our neighbor of his own, nor can we live and grow without that which is his. From this, our Lord takes what is humanly owed. For we ourselves are the temple, and what He takes from it is rightly of the sacrifice of Christ. So you also did not want to give bread and wine for His sake, for it is the bread of God the Father; therefore, He gives us that which is His. Now, He held nothing on earth but His body and blood. But if wine and bread are before our eyes, let it be that the bread is of no use, but rather the spirit is present in the bread and wine. For we eat a spiritual flesh—not taken from Mary, but a flesh that is spiritual. <note>This reflects a specific theological view called "Celestial Flesh," suggesting Christ's body was of a heavenly substance rather than purely human flesh from Mary.</note> Thus, your mortal self and yet an immortal one at the same time, which He brought with Him from heaven into the Virgin Mary’s womb. And His Transfiguration was revealed to His three disciples, *Peter, James, and John*, on the mountain.

Thus, the prophets are fundamentally found within Christ’s Gospel, and the Gospel within them, so that it may stand as a unified council of purpose and nothing more.

<meta>This page continues from a theological discussion of the Lord's Supper and the transformation of the believer through the sacrament. # The Sixth Book on the Light
## of Nature.

There are two kinds of arts: those of Nature, and those learned in the Holy Spirit. Those who live by the Spirit do not serve Nature. The others, who do not live in the Holy Spirit, are grounded in Nature. For these unbelievers, God has prefigured such marvelous wonders that even if someone were ever so stubborn in their unbelief, these works would move them toward faith. For the more an unbeliever is grounded in the Light of Nature <note>The "Light of Nature" is a concept—popularized by Paracelsus—referring to the innate wisdom or physical laws implanted by God in the created world, which can be understood through observation and reason.</note>, the more he is experienced in the wonders of God, and thus an Eternal, irrefutable God must be recognized through His works. As Christ further says regarding this: "If you will not believe me, then believe my works." Therefore, Christ also gave so many parables <note>parabolas</note> from the Light of Nature; thus it is most fitting to recognize the mysteries <note>misteria</note> of Nature well, so that the analogies may be better understood. Therefore, Christ did not act contrary to Nature, but rather fulfilled those same works; what Nature can do through its natural course, the Lord Christ accomplished through His word. Thus, medicine makes one healthy through the power of Nature, yet now it can happen without delay through divine blessing <note>original Latin: "sine interuallo benedictione divina"</note>. But Christ makes one healthy simply <note>original Latin: "simpliciter," meaning directly or without intermediate tools</note> through the word. For He is the one of whom Sirach speaks in Chapter 38, saying that He lets medicine grow out of the earth; that is, He who creates medicine, or the Creator of medicine, about whom it is said He is the highest Physician, for in Him is the highest essence of the Light of Nature. Therefore, in this book, two types of analogies will be treated. Some analogies concern the people who also draw the Last Supper into analogy. Secondly, the Great Works <note>original Latin: "magnalia"</note> and Secrets of Nature <note>original Latin: "Arcana Naturae"</note>, which then touch upon the introduction of such analogies themselves. For these great works are prophecies set from the beginning of the world until the coming of Christ their Creator, and they endure until the end of the world. Doves—that is, the dove <note>original Latin: "h. e. Columba"</note>—are quite without care; they hatch no hardship for their young and worry nothing about the winter, but instead abandon flight. Snakes have their great prudence <note>or caution</note> in their ears; they bite their own medicine; they make stones for themselves against various accidents, and they cover themselves with various improvements of natural knowledge.
Ravenous wolves <note>original Latin: "Lupi rapaces"</note>, which eat <unclear>eßat</unclear>, are envious of man; they take and rob from man whatever they can.
So too is the sheep-tick <note>Schafsmad</note> loose, which may sit upon a person, deceiving them and knowing from them what it will. Now our Creator <insert>Christ</insert> did not want a powerful analogy with the others or together, for they are of one nature, though not of one being.
But bread cannot be an analogy for Christ’s suffering, since it has neither His nature nor His property, nor does it work in that way; and even the most unbelieving person would find that the Passover Lamb <note>Osterlambt</note> would have been an analogy of Him, if Christ had ordained it so.
The Lamb of God <note>original Latin: "Agnis Dei," likely a misspelling of "Agnus Dei"</note> is a true analogy, not because of its form, but because of its nature; for God gave the lamb its character, therefore His Son must be the Lamb: simple, rich in heart, and of living character.
This, however, is not to be understood the same way regarding the bread.

**Light of the world** <note>original: *Lux mundi*</note>, for just as light is a guide for man, so also are the Apostles lights and guides for human souls. For man has let the soul see through the Apostles. But how can the wine and the blood of Christ be so dissimilar? The property of wine is all that is noble, while Christ’s property is all <unclear>lowly/veiled</unclear> <note>original: *hültl*, possibly meaning "wrapped" or "humble" in contrast to "noble."</note>: how can the one provide an analogy for the other? It would follow that the flesh of Christ were no better than the bread. But Christ says of the bread and the Body (not of the outward appearance), "I remain in you, and you in me."

**Salt of the earth** <note>original: *Sal terrae*</note>, what food is good without salt? In the same way, what man is righteous without salt, if he does not follow the Apostles in the flesh? The Apostles turn the flesh toward holiness. For their teaching and example deceive in nothing. For God salts the flesh of the earth through them, where there is no <unclear>sourness/corruption</unclear> <note>original: *sauer*, likely referring to the "leaven" of sin or the souring of rot.</note> that remains. He now takes it through the Apostles. The salt is in all the world; thus the Apostles must be received. Salt protects against rot. Thus, through the Apostles, one is embalmed **unto eternal life** <note>original: *ad vitam aeterna*</note>, just as the flesh of all animals is **preserved and conserved** <note>original: *praeservati conserviret*</note> through Jewish salt. The Apostles are not the salt themselves, but their teaching is like the salt.

But bread and Christ can be joined together neither in word <note>original: *dictione*</note> nor in meaning <note>original: *sententz*</note>, nor by nature, nor by **properties** <note>original: *h. e. proprietatibus*</note>. Christ did not say there, "**My Body**" <note>original: *Meum Corpus*</note>, or "**this body is My Body**" <note>original: *hoc corpus est Corpus meum*</note>. That would be an analogy. He did not say, "I am the bread as I have it in my hand." That would be an analogy. Rather, He is the **True Vine** <note>original: *Vitis Vera*</note>, which is also a proper analogy. For just as the grapevine is pleasant to all people, and love and community are a refreshment among all people, so also should there be great love and hope in Christ, and it should be better than all wine. Therefore, it is a proper analogy, through which we may recognize the use of His blood. Thus we find many analogies which, in this understanding, give way. Therefore, all figures of speech <note>original: *tropisch*, referring to "tropes" or metaphorical language.</note> arise from human understanding and remain within it.

But in the words of the Last Supper, Christ did not establish human nature; rather, He established faith, love, and the bitter death of His holy Testament’s covenant and memorial. Therefore, He used no light of nature as a human addition there. How then can such a thing be established, that our comparison should be between that which is from above and that which is from below—**that is** <note>original: *h. e.*, abbreviation for *hoc est*</note> the natural, which is human understanding, with the Divine Word?

**Salt**, the preaching and prophecy according to the content of the Gospel of God. The Magic <note>In this context, *Magia* refers to a spiritual mystery or the hidden, supernatural power of God working through the Word, rather than sorcery.</note> is not flesh but a mystery <note>original: *Mysterij*</note>. For the prophets proclaim that which concerns the Son of God. Just as the prophets, beyond nature, have prophesied the course of nature and the influence of the heavens, so the Gospels also have their own [influence]; they do not shine forth from the natural influence of the heavens, but they are the wisdom of God. And all other things are otherwise without His mystery. Thus are they also ordered in our time by those who contemplate them. Therefore, whoever does not believe, let him remain with the Word...

The virgin with the water in the sieve, which remained inside it, signifies the birth of Christ from a Virgin. <note>The "Virgin with the Sieve" is a classical emblem of chastity, originally referring to the Vestal Virgin Tuccia, here adapted to represent the miraculous nature of the Virgin Birth.</note>

<margin>PHOENIX</margin>
The phoenix has such <term>magnalia<note>From the Latin for "great things"; refers to the wonderful, hidden powers of God implanted in nature.</note></term> within it: It gathers dry wood together when the burden of old age weighs it down. It makes a hollow in the middle and finds a stone; with this, it flies up to the highest point above all birds, and then shines down like a beam into the wood. It ignites it all around the outside, and then as it burns underneath, the phoenix gazes into the air and thus burns itself to ashes. From those same ashes, a young phoenix lives again. This is now beyond all Nature and signifies these words: that the "old man" born of Adam must be burned from above and die completely in the state of Adam, and be born anew from water and spirit. This refers to the words of Christ to Nicodemus, so that they may be better understood (John 3:3), where He says: "Unless someone be born anew of water and Spirit, otherwise he cannot enter the Kingdom of God." You know that being born anew—likewise: what is born of the spirit, that is spirit.

The Lion <gloss>or: The Lioness</gloss> stands over its young when they are born and cries out so powerfully and strongly that the young come to life through it. <note>A common medieval belief was that lion cubs were born dead and brought to life after three days by the father's roar—a symbol of Christ's Resurrection.</note> This is now also nearly the way of nature. And the Lion is the most fierce and terrifying beast over man. The voice signifies the Last Day, when we shall be fearfully awakened by the voice of God for the judgment. Therefore, through these <term>magnalia</term>, the resurrection is better understood; and let it be said to you: if God gave such power to the lion alone to awaken his offspring's form, then we too shall be awakened. Thus Christ proved Himself true God with the raising of Lazarus by His voice. And He also gave Peter that power.

The Bear gives birth to its young without form; and it has the <term>magnalia</term> and the capacity within it to form them with its tongue. <note>A traditional natural history myth that mother bears "licked their cubs into shape."</note> This signifies that we are nothing from the mother's womb. Therefore, we must first be properly formed by another mother. Likewise, it is a prophecy of the New Birth: that we must be melted down into a new form, otherwise there would be nothing good in us.

<margin>PELICAN</margin>
The Pelican is also beyond nature: for its blood is food and drink <gloss>for</gloss> awakening its dead young. But it is also a prophecy of the Last Supper of Christ, that He will feed His own with His own blood, just as the pelican feeds its young. Thus Christ's teaching is also seemingly unnatural and wonderful to our understanding. Therefore, if such <term>magnalia</term> did not exist, then it would not be so with Christ, and vice versa. For all such things are arranged by Christ for the sake of man. And the <term>mysterium</term> (mystery) or <term>magnalia</term> are many more, which are known to a <term>Heilweise<note>Literally "Holy-Sage" or "Healing-Wise"; a term for a physician-philosopher who understands the divine secrets of nature.</note></term>. A part of them must be revealed. All of which are given to the common man and the unbeliever like a [closed] book.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of how the natural world serves as a mirror for spiritual mysteries. So that the light may shine for you, nature reveals that not all things are as they appear to the eye. Our eyes see the form of bodies as they are presented to us. Thus, everything we eat and drink is [potentially] all flesh and blood, but we do not see it as such. Therefore, we should not always place our trust in our sight; the same applies to our senses, for we see [food] clearly, and yet it is [destined to be] flesh and blood. Beef is coarse flesh and not human; however, when it is eaten by a human, it transforms within that person’s body into human flesh and blood. Likewise, all legumes <note>A term for beans, peas, and lentils, which were often discussed in early science regarding their nutritional "potency."</note> and other things that serve as food are, in a <term>mystery<note>In this context, a "mystery" refers to a hidden natural process ordained by God that is not immediately visible to the senses.</note></term>, human flesh in <term>potentia<note>A Latin philosophical term meaning "in potential." The author argues that food is not yet flesh, but has the hidden power to become it.</note></term>. As the wine and the drink [are mentioned] in the Scriptures, we drink blood; all this is spoken of through the "final matter" <note>The "final matter" (ultima materia) refers to the finished state of a substance after it has undergone its complete transformation.</note>.

Furthermore: all things have become the Body from the earth, and they take their physical forms from it. Now, the fruit of the Earth comes from above <note>Likely referring to the influence of the heavens or rain/sunlight on the growth of crops.</note>, and the Earth provides the physical body. Thus, a human becomes nothing without that same fruit which sustains them; but that same fruit transforms everything into flesh and blood, since nothing can come [to be] except from the earth. 

Initially, when we are conceived and born, we are neither blood nor flesh, for in the mother’s womb there is neither [fully formed] flesh nor blood; rather, we receive the human body’s form from the seed alone. When we are born, the mother’s milk provides our food and drink, coming from her own blood and flesh, and [becoming] everything that is within us. But once we outgrow the milk, we are strengthened in our body like a tree that has its essence from water; we then sustain our body through food, [drawing] the "Great World" into the "Small World." <note>This refers to the concept of the Macrocosm (the universe/nature) and the Microcosm (the human being). Humans "eat" the world to sustain their own smaller version of it.</note> For all other things serving as food and drink are nothing else than the body of man [in potential].

Therefore, no one should wonder how bread and wine [can be] the body and blood of Christ. Since it has now been said that every food and drink becomes our flesh and blood, anyone can say of any food or drink: "This is my body and blood." When it is in the stomach and becomes flesh, this truth is revealed, even if your eyes do not perceive it so clearly. For God the Father has 
<margin>everything</margin> 
intended to feed us in all the world through the body, within the manifoldness of the world, and it becomes the internal body within our stomachs.

In this same way, Christ, who is a man, can also point to bread and wine and say that it is his body and blood; for he certainly also possessed a human body and blood, just like other men.

Consider an example. Suppose I had my nourishment and my needs met through a daily, ordered serving of food and drink, which would become my flesh and blood. Now, a hungry and thirsty person unexpectedly comes to me. Before I eat, I give him half of my daily portion. Could I not say: "That is my body and my blood"? For I am giving him my very substance—from my own physical support—and not from some other person's substance, but from my own supply of food.

The Lord also testifies to this in Mark 12:43. When that <note>original: "Verna illa paupercula" (that poor little servant-woman/widow)</note> poor woman put two mites into the treasury <note>original: "gazophylacium"</note>, he said to his disciples: "Truly, the poor woman has put in more than all the others." For she gave alms from her entire substance; that is, she gave a part of her own body. That is called love truly perfected in a human: when one gives from one's own body, as has been described.

# Book VII.
## On the Worthy Use of the Lord’s Supper

So that we may observe the Lord’s Supper <note>original: *Nachtmall*</note> worthily, the teaching of Paul to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 10:17 and following) must be well understood. For there we do not have mere symbols, but the true flesh and blood of Christ, through which we are either glorified or condemned. Therefore, we must take careful note of two things:

1. That we cleanse the Lord's Supper <note>original: *Coenam Domini*</note> from all kinds of idolatry <unclear>cleanse</unclear>.
2. That we understand the true foundation of why we enjoy the Lord's Supper of Christ.

The first point does away with ceremonies and idolatrous teachings. This first point concerns the addition to and the alteration of the [divine] order. For the Remembrance <note>The "Remembrance" refers to the "Do this in remembrance of me" (Anamnesis) of the Eucharist.</note> has been <unclear>stripped</unclear> of its <unclear>standing</unclear>, broken by change and addition. Therefore, it should not take place in any temple. For here, the idols are made of wine; the altar is a piece of idolatry; the pomp that is used is a mockery of the suffering of Christ. Thus, all idolatrous clothing and vestments <note>original: *ornat*</note> should also be discarded. Likewise, we should flee the hands and voices of those same persons <note>Likely referring to the clergy of the established churches.</note>.

Regarding the second: the proclamation <note>original: *verkündigung*</note> should be done in such a way that we go forth in power to the unbelievers and proclaim his death. Among believers, it is not necessary. For those who believe in the death of Christ also believe in everything else.

Now, note an interpretation of these two points. The idolatrous call it a "Sacrament" upon which they give it; they proclaim the death of Christ without a proper place. Their heart is far from their mouth, and from their singing and speaking; therefore, it is a dead proclamation from which no fruit grows. Yet the true remembrance lies in the heart, and the true proclamation is in the mouth. The power of the heart is love in Christ. But the love of the heart drives the tongue toward the unbelievers to proclaim the death of the Lord Christ.

Now, in times of need, friends are tested.
<margin>but not worthily</margin>
The true [friends] are those against the idolatrous lot. Hold yourselves according to the Apostles, and see how He regards His friends who stayed with Him in His time of need.

Now they give the sacrament for this purpose, and in receiving it, they eat together. They are divided in two. One considers worldly things, another his money, property, interest, and fields, another his children, and so they remain unchanged in their old ways. For just as their hearing of the Word of God is, so also is their fruit and their thought. They lash themselves a little in the church, but outside, when <term>occasions</term> <note>original: *Occasiones*; meaning favorable circumstances or opportunities to sin or pursue worldly gain.</note> arise, they chase after these things. And thus, they forget the <term>boundaries</term> <note>original: *termini*; the spiritual limits or the specific terms/definitions set by Christ.</note> of Christ. And they divide one another. Thus, they play games with the flesh and blood of Christ.

The highest point of the Lord's Supper is that we put away the love that is only in the mouth and drive all things into the hearts of men. Therefore, the right order is that those come together who wish to proclaim the death of Christ to the unbelievers, and they should eat with one another in their houses, breaking bread; finally, they bless the Lord. They then eat his body and drink his blood, and sing his song of praise to the Lord. From this follows the keeping of his commandment. Stand in every word, and proclaim the [death of the Lord].

Faith does everything in this eating and drinking, for it is not a food for the fingers <note>A metaphor for physical, tactile consumption versus spiritual belief.</note>. The memory and proclamation of Christ’s death is held equally among the holy. These things should not just go along with each other, but Christians themselves should remember that the holy Gospel and the Father have been proclaimed to them—the Word of God—so that they might come to it. Therefore, they should remember it, and desire to be brought to remembrance and memory, so that they all might become steadfast in faith, and remain in Him, and do His will; which also proceeds through the power of the spirit that makes one alive. For to remember, to know, and yet [still] have to do [it], that is eternal death; but the confession of Christ, faith, and love, acting according to the teaching of Christ, is eternal life, as Paul also says.

Therefore, this Lord's Supper <note>original: *abendtmall*</note> shall be held apart from all idolatry, appearance, pomp, and the prestige of persons. It is solely for the memory of Christ—of His suffering, death, and total satisfaction <note>The theological concept that Christ's sacrifice was sufficient to pay for all sins.</note>—which happens only in the believing heart, and not with the simple hall <note>Possibly referring to the physical room or the earthly assembly.</note> and the eating and drinking.

For in the place of Christ, there is no hindered spirit or our confession and desire for [forgiveness of] sins. From this, we have our only refuge on Earth solely in the body and blood of Christ, in which the spiritual [grace] flows, which makes us alive; in that, the food is created for us. Therefore, it follows that we are all His, and remain equally in Christ. May God graciously help us in this. Amen.

# ON THE ETERNAL LIMBO <note>original Latin: *De Limbo Æterno*; "Limbo" here likely refers to a boundary or state of being between the mortal and the eternal.</note>
## and the perpetual New Man of the second creation,
## from Christ the Son of GOD.

All philosophers who have been enlightened in the Light of Nature <note>A common term in mystical philosophy referring to the innate knowledge of the physical and spiritual world accessible to human reason.</note> have diligently perceived and described the natural moisture of all things, their powers, and their works. In the same way, nearly many a student of nature <note>original: *Naturküner*</note> has also labored to ascribe virtues [to things], and has successfully settled many a small contradiction. For one who has recognized their natural things can hardly let go of them; for the longer he recognizes them and feeds into them, the more he finds a joyful growth and result. Therefore, he not only loves them dearly, but survives them, and may deem them worthy of being loved for eternity as part of his inner portion. But what is it now, even if such a person searched the entire sphere of all natural things and could understand them all correctly, yet finds that all nature is mortal and subject to all corruption? Whoever considers this rightly (as is fitting) will find the mind of the physicist <note>term: *physico* — here meaning a natural philosopher or student of the physical world.</note> becomes troubled; for he sees death not only around man (though it is most gruesome in him) but also in all things closest to him, which are cast down and rot, however fine the flower may be. Therefore, the physicist also receives a different spirit, no longer merely to follow or research nature, but he begins to investigate the mortal foundation for that which is not subject to death. This is now the true philosophy.

Hereupon is now my noble intent: to be concerned with mortal being and research the eternal glows <note>original: *loehen*; likely referring to spiritual flames or the "burning" light of divine power.</note> and powers that exist without any death. For even if these are well-founded through and through in the Light of Nature, there remains for us only a path toward death; the course of nature remains deathly. Therefore, it is of the highest necessity for us to seek after the Eternal Light which remains with us even in death, and we also with it, and how we may attain an immortal life after this one. This is the stone of "Super-Comprehensibility," sweetness, and eternal joy.

It is more significant that after the creation of the first man, the children were divided in many ways and fell away from great understanding and dedicated themselves to other things, which they then did not learn from their parents. The cause is that in many, the eternal was abandoned, and nothing was valued of the soul; they meant that the body and the soul were a single thing and thus die [together]. And it is not only this erroneous form, but many more besides, that men have come to, which are not right to describe. But despite all that, the Light of Nature gives a proof-light in man beforehand, in <unclear>ways</unclear> and a mortal [one]. For when one considers the beginning of man—that he is formed after the Image of God—that same Image must be immortal and perceptible; and further, all things of the firmament and the elements become mortal, but man does not.

### Methods for a New Philosophy: From the Mortal to the Immortal.

If there is such a great delight to be drawn from Natural Philosophy <note>The study of the physical world through observation and reason</note>, how much more so in the philosophy of the Kingdom of God, where God the Creator of Nature Himself dwells. For the more philosophy is recognized and refined, the more the Spirit is prepared for it. Nonetheless, the ancient philosophers arrived blind in Nature and rose high in the light of worldly wisdom, but the Cornerstone <note>A reference to Christ as the foundation of all truth (Ephesians 2:20)</note> and the root from which the Eternal Man grows, they did not know. Therefore, they believed all the more firmly in mortality. For they had no experience of the eternal—

<margin>
If Plato had lived at the time of Christ and had believed, what would I give—since he reached so high in the light of Nature—how powerfully he would have grasped the Eternal.
</margin>

—ity.

<margin>
Since I am now like Plato, yet have no foundation but the Gospel alone, the Word of God, and the Eternal from which I write—though I have put death upon it <note>likely meaning he has disciplined his mortal self</note> so that they might experience an Eternal within Man. Should he [Plato] still live and have that eternal foundation, how strongly would such things have been written about the Eternal by them.
</margin>

In this way, Aristotle lost himself in his own fantasy within the Light of Nature; he took up morals and virtues, attempting to grasp them as far as his poor findings in the Light of Nature allowed. But I say all his teaching is as nothing for Christians. For where true understanding is not present, there can be no right philosophizing, unless one possessed the writings of the Christians concerning Christ.

<margin>Therefore</margin>
Since true philosophy is now among us Christians, I may well say there are very few Christians who trouble themselves with it. Even if they do, people still use the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle, and yet they do not treat those concepts in a Christian manner. This does not happen without harm. Virgil was a pagan, yet in his books—the *Eclogues*, the *Georgics*, and <unclear>Theode:</unclear> <note>Possibly a reference to Theocritus, or a misreading of another title</note>—he wrote more of the Christian faith than all the poets of the Christians. If he were compared to our poets, which teacher who names more poets would be his equal?

People want to read Cicero in *On Duties* <note>original: "in officijs"</note> and *Cato*, which show great brilliance and piety. Had he possessed the Christian foundation, how magnificent and noble his *Paradoxes* would be. I have written the same regarding Seneca, as all those who began in piety also directed others toward it. But the very life of truth is Boethius, who proved enough for a Christian; he grasped the faith from a pagan foundation and understood it in a Christian way. As did Francesco Petrarch after him.

If I busy myself with uncovering the Eternal Man, the cause is that many sleep and lie in a dream. Neither Heraclitus, nor Seneca, nor Pythagoras have yet fallen into this sleep, but certainly they have already risen. For they would have had the right foundation of their eternal right and a light. This foundation would surely drive away sleep. It would drive them day and night, like water drives mill wheels.

First, we must know the reason why Christ our Lord commanded us to eat His body and to drink His blood: and why He has placed salvation so much within the preparation <term>rüstung</term> <note>This term refers to the spiritual state of readiness or "equipping" oneself to receive the sacrament.</note> of His body or flesh and blood. Although it is often shown by what means and ways one comes to salvation, and how they have now passed into one another, yet none is separated from the other because of it. Rather, all are in the [same] way, and it is nothing more than this: he who believes and is baptized shall be saved. Just as he who loves God and his neighbor as himself shall be saved. Likewise: Blessed are the poor in spirit. Blessed are the meek. Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of Christ's name. Blessed are those who weep and those who suffer. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the spiritual necessity of the Sacrament. Thus, without the flesh and blood of Christ—the second, heavenly Adam—no person can ever find a way to heaven. Therefore, there are two births: the first into this world, and the other into heaven.

You should understand these two births in this way: just as we were born of Adam into this earthly world, so too will we be born of Christ into heaven on that day. For a child of Christ to be born into that heavenly kingdom, Christ must be his Father, and this happens in no other way than through that very birth. That is to say, He is the Father of all His children, in that He gives birth to them for salvation through His own flesh and blood.

And so, the second birth comes from Christ through the Supper—for which He so heartily longed—when He ate with His disciples. There, He gave them His flesh and blood to eat and to drink. Through this eating, they were born a second time. This is the second birth of the children who come from Christ into the Kingdom of God, for which (as stated above) He so heartily yearned. 

And this is why: just as Adam was established by God as the forefather of his descendants, and they in turn of theirs—and as it was ordained that humanity should be propagated <term>propagiren: to reproduce or multiply</term> in this earthly world through the seed, with all the necessities belonging to our nature and existence—all of which comes with and must continue through the seed. In the same way, Christ wants us to be born a second time. He gives us His flesh and blood to eat and drink essentially, truly, and visibly; materially and substantially <term>materialisch Substantialisch: technical terms arguing that Christ is physically present in the bread and wine, not just symbolically</term>, and not merely in spirit (as the "enthusiastic" dreamers <note>original: "Schwermerisch phantasten"; a derogatory term used by reformers for those who viewed the Sacraments as purely symbolic or spiritual rather than physical.</note> imagine). 

Rather, it is just as physical as the way we are born into this world from natural parents in a complete and worldly manner through the seed. And so it is that we are physically born into heaven through the flesh and blood of Christ. Whoever does not have this birth will not be saved. For it was once decided, established, and ordained by God that just as one is born humanly from the seed into this world, and possesses that birth, so should and must we be born once more into heaven through the flesh and blood of Christ, which we must receive truly physically, and not just in spirit. 

Therefore, the distribution of the Supper is described thus: that Christ gave it to the disciples in the bread—which gives way to it <note>original: "dz sich davon loßt"; possibly suggesting the substance of the bread yielding to the substance of Christ's body.</note>—and likewise in the wine. It was not commanded to be received merely in spirit. For the second birth must happen within our own flesh and blood, and it happens through Christ, just as physical birth happens through the seed of man. 

And just as the seed of Adam has born all people from Adam, so Christ has born a second time through His flesh and blood all those whom He finds ordained for salvation. Whoever does not have this birth will not be saved; that is, he cannot be saved. Just as a natural person cannot exist without a father's seed, so too can no one among us be saved without the flesh and blood of Christ. This is the reason why the second birth is so important. For Christ is not fashioned to redeem anyone other than His children—no one else. Whosoever is His child, he redeems. Therefore, He is the Father who redeems His own. And those are His children who are born a second time through His flesh and blood. So shall...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Gospel of John, chapter 6, moving from the miraculous feeding of the five thousand and the crossing of the sea to Christ’s discourse on the "Bread of Life." It maintains the previous page's focus on the distinction between the "belly-fillers" (those seeking material gain) and the true spiritual followers.</meta>

## ...thus from the loaves with which you were filled. Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which remains into eternal life. <note>original Latin: *sic ex panibꝰ q̄ saturati estis. Operamini nō cibū qui perit, sed q̄ pmanet in vitā æternā.* A paraphrase of John 6:26-27.</note>

Christ does not regard those listeners who only seek the filling of their bellies <note>German: *bauch fülle*. This refers to those who focus on physical appetite and material satisfaction rather than spiritual truth.</note> and follow him merely to make him a king, seeking great authority and an easy life. He regards only those who do not forget the miracle of the bread: which is exactly what the "belly-fillers" do. Instead, they should look upon the signs they have seen, and through them give him their faith—knowing that he is not there to feed their bellies with perishable food, but to feed them with the eternal food. This food does not pass through the belly, but remains in us until eternity without end. This same food shall be prepared for you, which the Son of Man will give.

**Which the Son of Man will give to you.** <note>original Latin: *Quem Filius hōis dabit vobis.* From John 6:27.</note>

This food, which my son, the <term>Son of Man</term> <note>In this context, the author uses "Son of Man" to emphasize Christ's shared nature with humanity, which allows humans to partake in his divinity.</note>, shall give to you, comes in no other way; otherwise, he would have given it [only] at the Last Supper. Therefore, it must remain centered on the Supper. Thus, the flesh must remain with those to whom he gave it—not as a filling of the belly, but as a bread that has come down from heaven spiritually, as he said: "This is my body." Now, the physical bread did not literally fall from the sky. But the point is: "This is my body." That is the essence of what he said. If one wishes to look at it merely superficially, the bread did not come from heaven, but from the baker. However, he upholds <term>physics</term> <note>original: *physicam*. Here meaning the natural order of creation.</note> much better: for in that sense, the bread *did* come from heaven, because all things have come forth from the mouth of God. And where is God, if not in heaven? Therefore, whatever has come into being through His words is from heaven, even if the material from which it is made is earthly. From what else did the earth itself come? From nothing other than the voice of God. Thus, in the beginning, all things are from God. From the earth come all plants, and the human being follows: therefore, Adam was a Son of God. For he was made from the voice of God, and he was meant to be obedient to that voice, and not to the dictates of flesh and blood. So too with the bread that becomes venerable among us—does it not originate from the voice of God? Could not the Spirit take that same bread and say: "This is that which his father made for man out of the earth"? Yes, for that very reason, the bread is that which is from above, which brings our souls to eternal life; it is that same bread that does not spoil. It is not a filling of the belly, but an eternal food.

Since he now distinguishes between the two types of food—the food for the belly and the eternal food—which the hand of the Son of Man gives, he calls himself the "Son of Man" so that we may understand that we also share in his being. Thus, this food must be a different kind of food than simple bread—namely, the grain of which he speaks. And even if it is not [physically] visible like the blessed Adam, it is nonetheless invisible like the soul, which is the true essence of the human being.

**For him God the Father has sealed.** <note>original Latin: *Hunc n̄ pater signavit Deus.* From John 6:27.</note>

Therefore, God has confirmed him; he is the bread that He has blessed as His creation. Rather, let the bread be the "Earth" from which the Son of God comes, who makes us gods.

### Jesus then said to them: "Truly, truly I say to you: It was not Moses who gave you the bread from Heaven; but my Father gives you the true bread from Heaven." <note>original: *Dixit ergo eis JHESUS, Amen Amen dico Vobis. Non Moses dedit panem de Cœlo: Sed pater meus dat vobis panem de Cœlo Verum.* From John 6:32.</note>

Moses gave this bread <note>referring to the manna in the wilderness</note>, but where did he get it? Namely, from God. He [God] gave it to Moses and did not want Moses to say that he [Moses] had it [by his own power], so that the honor and the praise would belong to Him [God]. For God works in many ways through His servant.

As for the bread that we have <note>original: *dz weyse hab'*, likely referring to the manner in which the faithful possess spiritual bread</note>, I did not receive it from God [as a separate gift], nor from Moses. For Christ is God, who has given it from within Himself. How much greater then is this than the bread of Moses, who was only a human being, like a servant?

### For the true bread is he who comes down from Heaven and gives life to the world. <note>original: *Panis n[ost]er Verus qui de Cœlo descendit, & dat Vita mundo.* From John 6:33.</note>

Therefore He speaks: the bread is God's, not Moses'. It is not for the servant's benefit to use for eating and devouring, but for God Himself. For He alone is the one to whom honor and praise belong; it is God’s bread, not Moses’ bread—bread that is begotten from heaven. And that same manna indeed descended and fell from heaven. But it did not come from that [Highest] Heaven from which His glory descended. But the bread that has descended from the true Heaven gives life to the world. 

What is this "world"? Not only the Jews, but also the Gentiles. Not only the Greeks, but also the Germans <note>original: *teutsch*</note>. That is what "the world" means: those to whom this bread (which is what Christ signifies) gives their portion <note>original: *loß*</note>. For the Jews are not meant alone; they would not even make up a fifth part of what is intended here. By "the world" understood here, it means everyone through and through. Therefore, the Bread of the Word <term>Bread of the Word (German: *brodt wordtt*) refers to Christ as the living message or Logos of God</term> surpasses the Jews' bread.

### Then they said to him: "Lord, give us this bread always." <note>original: *Dixerunt ergo ad eum Semper da nobis panem hunc.* From John 6:34.</note>

At that moment, a certain pleasing devotion came upon them, stemming from the day of Christ's suffering. Therefore, notice that the human spirit is a living sense, and it becomes sick if it does not hold onto what is ordained by God. Then the Devil runs in and interferes, so that at one moment there is good understanding, and at another, evil. 

Likewise, in another respect, <term>free will (*freÿe wille*)</term> is recognized. For the [worldly] wise will not be able to "borrow" hatred [or choose] whether to believe in God or not. But Christians have the free will of the Spirit of Christ, which is what leads us there, just as wisdom does. But the wise have God’s obedience, and therefore they are a people held captive in His hand. But the Christian has a free will; the reason is they may act outwardly as [the Spirit] breaks into them. Sometimes it stands, and sometimes it does not. So it was with these Jews too; previously they were with Christ, but now the spirit has taken another turn <note>original: *loage*, likely *Lage* or position</note>, and they want the bread all the time for that reason.

### Jesus said to them: "I am that bread of life. He who comes to me shall not hunger, and he who believes in me shall never thirst." <note>original: *Dixit autem eis Jhesus Ego sum Ille panis Vitæ. Qui Venit ad me, non esuriet, et qui Credit in me, non sitiet in æternum.* From John 6:35.</note>

Since they were now so eager, Christ pointed out the bread to them—that he himself was the bread, the bread of life, of which [he spoke] previously.

## "Is this not the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then does he say: 'I came down from heaven'?" <note>original: *Nonne hic ē filius Joseph, cuius nos, nouimus patrem et matrem? Quomodo ergo dixit hic Quia de Coelo descedi?* From John 6:42.</note>

Then the envious spirit fell back into them again, and it spread once more throughout the congregation, each person for himself and yet all finding fault with his claim that he should be a bread come down from heaven. For no one believed that a person become flesh could be a bread come down from heaven! Unless one is taught by God, which is to be understood only by the elect. Such a person could understand. If not, then you do not understand it. But the Jews understood only that he was born of Joseph. So it was with the Jews. They recognized him only as a <term>carpenter</term> <note>original: *Zimmermann*. ## "Jesus therefore answered and said to them: 'Do not murmur among yourselves. No one can come to me unless the Father, who sent me, draws him. ## "Everyone therefore who has heard from the Father and has learned, comes to me. Not that anyone has seen the Father, except he who is from God; he has seen the Father. Amen Amen dico vobis: Qui credit in me habet vitam æternam. Ego sum panis vitæ.* From John 6:45-48.</note>

Can God teach in person? It cannot be. For no one has seen God the Father, except the Son. Now it stands written in the prophets: "All shall be taught wisdom by God." Therefore one must learn wisdom from God, and yet not see Him, but still learn wisdom from Him. This brings much cause for dispute among those who lack reason. Whoever learns wisdom from him—it is a hidden teaching that sits within us, and no one knows how it remains in us. For thus it is: since no one sees the <term>schoolmaster</term> <note>original: *Schulmeister*. A metaphor for God the Father as the internal instructor of the soul.</note>, no one sees the lesson either. And yet the schoolmaster and the lesson lead to wisdom. 

Now, as he says: he who trusts and believes in me has eternal life. But to trust him is to believe his words. For faith cannot exist without trust; from trust springs faith. Therefore, whoever truly trusts me has eternal life. Trust brings love; love proves faith. If we do not trust Christ, then we do not believe him either; thus we do not have love for him, so that we might accept what he gives us.

## Jesus said to them: "Truly, truly, I say to you: Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink His blood, you will not have life in yourselves. Whoever eats the bread of Christ <gloss>as the belly and the mouth [do]</gloss> and drinks His blood has eternal life." For a person only enters Heaven if they have come from Heaven. Thus, the [natural] person is nothing but the body; therefore, they do not go to Heaven. But whoever eats the bread sees the flesh from Heaven.

## "And I will raise you up on the last day." <note>original: "Et ego resuscitabo vōs in nouissimo die" (John 6:54b)</note>

Therefore, the resurrection is achieved in the Son, not in the Father.

## "For My flesh is truly food, and My blood is truly drink. ...Mary’s womb: and from that same body, which was born of Mary, eat the bread of the body in the Lord’s Supper, which for both bodies is the resurrection of eternal life. ### Many of His disciples, upon hearing this, said: "This is a hard saying." <note>original: "Multi ergo ex discipulis eius audientes dixerunt Durus est Sermo iste" (John 6:60)</note>

Indeed, for those who understand things according to human reason and do not believe, it is a hard saying. Therefore, such a person does not believe until the time of the resurrection. For that reason, it is not a "hard saying" when spoken from the body of Jesus, which cannot be deceived. But whoever does not believe, rejects it; they do not understand through faith. It is likely that such a person will not listen at all, but will let Him go—not wanting to grant that He should take His bread from His own body, just as Eve was taken from Adam. <note>The author uses the "Adam and Eve" analogy to explain the Eucharist: just as Eve was formed from Adam’s side, the "Bread of Life" is formed from Christ’s flesh.</note> And if the bread is what He says it is, who would dare to question Him about it?

### But Jesus, knowing in Himself that His disciples were grumbling about this, said to them: "Does this offend you?" <note>original: "Sciens autem Ihesus apud semetipsum quod murmurarent de hoc discipuli eius dixit eis Hoc vos scandalizat" (John 6:61)</note>

It does not rightly trouble Him that this teaching should cause them <unclear>offense</unclear>, since they were His disciples and ought to have believed whatever He spoke. They believe other things that seem impossible: that He descended from Heaven, and spoke of flesh and blood in a manner that also creates His humanity. Since Christ is the one who can do this without harm to His person, He can also take the bread from His own body.

### What if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where He was before? <note>original: "Si ergo videritis filium hominis ascendentem ubi erat prius" (John 6:62)</note>

If this [the bread] cannot be believed, how would one believe in the resurrection in Christ—that He will arrive there after death, from where He first came forth? He who does not believe that what is below can rise up toward Heaven must also believe that if He is from Heaven, He must also return there. For it is one faith. What do we want to say to those who will be so harshly judged on the Last Day? They will claim to be believers then, but that same faith will be of no use to them. For what is the flesh? Nothing. But the Spirit of God makes all these things. Therefore, nothing more should be added to the flesh; only the Spirit of God makes alive and gives Life. The flesh can give nothing. For who can give life to a sinful being? No one can. He [the Spirit] alone grants that a person has flesh and blood. And it is the Spirit, as God the Son, who gives life. In that which lives, the flesh is useless, for it cannot give life; it is merely a mortal creature.

### The words that I have spoken to you are Spirit and they are Life. <note>original: "Verba quæ ego locutus sum vobis Spiritus sunt Et Vita sunt" (John 6:63)</note>

These are Spirit and they are Life; that is God. For God is a Spirit, and God is the life. From the Spirit all things spring forth and everything lives. Therefore, the words of Christ are life and they are Spirit, just as God Himself is. Therefore His word works what God works, and man does not.

# ON THE LORD’S SUPPER E 1. 3. 74.
## Chapter: Gospel of John: and this is the 17th point in the order

John the Evangelist has provided a Gospel and chapters out of his own spirit which he received from God. In that same spirit, he grasped the teaching and taught the beginning of the <term>second creature</term> <note>This refers to the "New Creation" or the spiritual transformation of a person through faith.</note>, from whence they come and where they took their beginning. Now, this description proves that John is an interpreter of the sacrifice and the <term>second birth</term> <note>Also known as being "born again," a central theme in John’s Gospel.</note> out of his distinct spirit. For he, and he alone, spoke much regarding this second birth. Thus, John also applied his spirit to this and gave us to understand Christ according to his spirit—how Christ is wise in him and He is in us—so that he might sustain us with words of teaching and the birth from the Mother, which Christ spoke of to Nicodemus. <note>A reference to John 3, where Jesus tells Nicodemus he must be born again of water and the spirit.</note> If John had not written of the second birth and the teaching of the second creature, and had left it behind for us, we would have no vision of the second birth in his spirit from the number of styles, which would have also given us to understand what he held to be true. What John received from it, and how it is to be understood and accepted: thus he ordered his spirit and interpreted it.

Therefore, we should all rightly regard this spirit of this man—who is sent by God—as the one to follow. For since he is such a man who teaches for our sake and interprets in this way, such a wise man and such a human Christian spirit should also go forth and teach us to keep the way of teaching, and to learn and have faith, just as this Evangelist teaches and instructs us out of his own spirit as a man gifted by God. For his wisdom is taught through this Evangelist as a man sent from God, unlike any other. Rather, it is well said: "God's holy spirits." Therefore, we should accept this last chapter of the Evangelist John with great understanding. <note>Though the header mentions the 17th point, the author is introducing the foundational "Light" of John's theology.</note> For there he concludes an enlightened teaching. Because of this, he is rightly called an **Eagle** <note>In Christian iconography, the Four Evangelists are assigned symbols; John is the Eagle because his theology is perceived as "soaring" to the highest spiritual heights.</note> among all the Evangelists. For none among all the Evangelists flew higher in the spirit than he, the Evangelist John; no one wrote more than he. For he concludes here the greatest points of the **New Birth**, which is the greatest enlightenment that the wise master places in our faith; upon this, it must be set and established. And if this first point is not brought home to us, then we lose all our things upon the sand. This reward is solely the Body which wisdom has from Christ: if we do not have that same body, then all our hope is gone.

> In the beginning was the Word: and the Word was with God: and God was the Word. This was in the beginning with God. <note>original Latin: "In principio erat Verbum: et Verbum erat apud Deum: et Deus erat Verbum. Hoc erat in principio apud Deum." This is the opening of the Gospel of John.</note>

Now the Evangelist proceeds to describe the beginning (as it is the custom of all scholars to describe the beginning of all things <gloss>in Christ</gloss> <note>original: "Christo"</note>, from whence comes the <margin>From here, see Book 1 of the Mirror, see verse 13. <note>original: "De hinc vide lib. 1 speculo. v. vide 13." This likely refers to a contemporary theological commentary or a specific edition of a text called the "Mirror."</note></margin><gloss>right understanding</gloss>:). Now he says: In the beginning was the Word. That is to say, in the beginning, everything was nothing. And there was nothing but a Word, which no one sees and which possesses no physical part. And that same Word was God himself; just as the Word of Christ is God himself, and is also Spirit and Life. For Word, Spirit, and Life are one thing, and they are God. Thus the beginning was with God, who made all things. This God, in all his work, used nothing else but his Word alone. Through the Word, he does all things. Therefore, the Word is the beginning of all things with God. 

In the same way that a craftsman is the beginning when he intends to build a work, or prepare wood for the fire—one might take up the wood to build with a <gloss>carpenter’s axe</gloss> or use <gloss>a scribe’s pen and ink</gloss>. In this way, the only instrument used by God is the Word, which is both the material of the same and everything else. From this we should understand that the liberation points toward Christ in such a way that his beginning, and the beginning of all his works and all things, is accomplished with the Word <gloss>without any other means</gloss>. The Word cleanses us; the Word makes the dead living. The Word drives out the devils. The Word heals all sicknesses. Now, since God the Father had nothing other than the Word as a beginning for all his works, as has been mentioned, we know from this that God has given all things in his Word. 

<margin>Rupert [of Deutz], Book Seven, Abbot, on the Victory of the Word. <note>original: "Rupert[us] Liber Septi- mus Abbatis de Victoria Verbi." Rupert of Deutz (c. 1075–1129) was an influential Benedictine theologian; "De Victoria Verbi Dei" (On the Victory of the Word of God) was one of his major works.</note></margin>Then, what we introduce of a single nature is attributed to his Word. It is as if the Evangelist says: God will not become one with the words of God as the enemies of the Word do, who [oppose] the Word with a natural hand: rather, with the Word alone is the work, the instrument, and the material. Thus God works, and yet he works nothing [physically]. For what a man does with his hand, God does with the Word and more besides. For God has all things in his hand and in his power, as is to be understood from the Godhead and is good to know.

### All things were made through him: and without him was nothing made. <note>original: "Omnia per ipsum facta sunt: et sine ipso factum est Nihil." (John 1:3)</note>

Since all things are made by God through the Word, there is nothing there that belongs to or originates from man. Therefore, it follows from this that man may not fathom how all things are created and come to be. Instead, let him remain with that which tells us that God is with God. And without God, nothing has come to be. All this signifies that we have one God, one Creator in all works, so that we need not bring anything else to it. Since all things came from God, we should not—nor will we, like the devil—desire to know how it might happen, or from what purpose. For these things are all to be sought with God, and not at all with man.

So we have the same word from Christ: "This is my Body; this is my blood." These words become blood and flesh in us, just as food becomes blood and flesh, upon that word; for there, flesh and blood have been created. This is Christ’s incarnation <term>menschwerdung: the process of God becoming human</term>. It depends upon the word, not upon the bread. In the word, the bread is found within, even if it were not fetched. Since it is indeed sufficient in the words, if someone were to say: "This is my Body," in that same faith. But the bread is taken from Christ, and so it remains. For the word makes the bread into the flesh and body of Christ. Thus we must enjoy it, with our teeth, for a better remembrance. The body of Christ was truly physical <note>original: "leiblich"</note> and yet not carnal <note>original: "fleischlich"; the author distinguishes between a "true body" and "worldly/sinful flesh"</note>, essential and not figurative, not airy, and not a fantasy. And just as a bread is to be eaten physically, and becomes blood and flesh, so should we enclose the words physically, and not let anyone take them from us. Therewith the bread and the word have come together, for a physical manifestation, and to become physical. Thus the word leads to flesh, just as it became flesh in Mary—it is also flesh, without carnal seed, solely through the word.

# Concerning the 3rd Chapter of the Gospel of John, Verse 3

<margin>Thus Christ proves the birth from above.</margin>
> "Unless one be born again, etc." <note>original Latin: "Nisi quis renatus fuerit denuo &c."</note>

Thus Christ proves the birth from above, as a creature <term>Creatur: here meaning a 'newly created being' or a soul transformed by God</term> whom you should no longer know, and says thus: Since all those who are to come into the kingdom of God or heaven must be born anew, that is, from above. <margin>Note: Bodily</margin> ...bodily into another creature. For the first one is worth nothing; it is lost and brought to nothing. Therefore, another birth must be there, and this same birth is from above. Therefore, Christ sets this ever higher, so that we should not regard the fact that we are of Adam, of flesh and blood. For all that is nothing before God. We should only strive toward being born from above, and think no further on any father or mother, nor put our trust, reliance, or hope in anyone, except only in that birth. Yet it is not to be understood otherwise than that we, above all things, must have a body for salvation <term>seligkeit: the state of being saved or eternal blessedness</term>. First all our things are forgiven. Therefore, it is to be most firmly <note>original: "am fasten", likely meaning "most fixedly" or "most certainly"</note> considered how we are born. In the same way as a person is first born naturally, and as a natural human being—afterward he has the strength and power to act as a human—but if he is not born as a human, then all subsequent things will fail and be nothing. So it is also for him who wishes to live Christianly in faith, hope, and the love of God; for him, that same [new life] must [arise?] <unclear>entsing.</unclear> from the body; where he does not have that same body, then everything he does is in vain. Therefore, Christ sets this at the very first as the beginning and salvation. This is simply the first article of birth: repentance <term>buß: the act of turning away from sin; penance</term> made into a Christian. This same birth comes from above. It also concerns the Lord from above. For otherwise there is no house, no more gates that may go from heaven to the earth or come to us, except only right Christians—we too, who are that second birth. For those who are of the earth, are of the earth. Those from heaven, are from heaven.

> "He cannot see the kingdom of God." <note>original Latin: "Non potest videre regnum Dei."</note>

Although man was placed in paradise as a creation, he was afterward taken and struck down. Since God has now, for the second time, sent His Friend <note>A reference to Christ</note> into the air within His creature—who is now from heaven to man, for he had to [leave] paradise—and because such a thing has happened, heaven is further determined: God no longer makes any creature out of the earth, no other <unclear>läuscher</unclear> <note>Possibly "listeners" or "lookouts," or a misspelling of "leute" (people)</note>. Rather, whatever He creates anew must be from heaven and must be from His seed, because He has no other friend. He will be more in His kingdom, which was opened up in repentance. For heaven must be pure and clean of this, otherwise no one enters heaven, unless he be of the body from heaven. That is, born from heaven. From that same birth, no enemy shall see the Lord God anymore.

> "Nicodemus said to him, 'How can a man be born again when he is old? Can he enter into his mother's womb [again]?'" <note>original Latin: "Dixit ad eum Nicodemus, quomodo potest homo renasci cum sit senex? Numquid potest in ventrem matris suae intro."</note>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Gospel of John, specifically the dialogue between Jesus and Nicodemus regarding the necessity of being "born again." It transitions from the physical limitations of Adam's lineage to the spiritual reality of the new birth through water and the Spirit.</meta>

...to enter and be born again. <note>original Latin: "introire ac renasci"</note> Nicodemus understood the birth rightly as a bodily one. For bodily it must happen in flesh and blood. In that case, a person must above all things believe and hold that the flesh which proceeds from Adam will pass away and does not enter into heaven; instead, we shall be of another flesh and blood, yet also tangible. But Nicodemus did not understand 

<margin>That one is not born from the seed of men, but out of God's power.</margin>

how one is born according to the Spirit, or how a person—according to the seed in every way—is born a second time, and he did not understand that the human being is made through God’s power. The old nature will no longer exist, but rather [the new exists] according to the seed of human blood and flesh: as a human ought to be. For in this alone is all good: that a human remains in human flesh and bodily form on earth, yet eats in heaven; and this happens not in Adam’s flesh and blood, but by coming into another body, blood, and flesh. That is now the second birth of which Christ speaks.

> Jesus answered: "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God." <note>original Latin: "Respondit Jhesus. Amen, Amen dico Vobis, Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non pt introire in regnum Dei."</note>

Here Christ reveals how this person is born: no longer from the nature of Adam, but from two things—namely, from water and the Spirit. The water is now the conception through the Holy Spirit, in which the Father then forms the one who is baptized. He who is thus baptized is now "water," and the Spirit of God comes over him, and he is born anew. And the "Jewish woman" <note>The author likely uses "the Jewish woman" as an allegorical reference to the physical lineage or perhaps the womb of the old law, which must be replaced by the spiritual "mother" of baptism.</note> is the second birth of man: truly the mother in which the human must be born anew for the second time, and not in the natural mother, but in water and Spirit. Here he must be <unclear>dead to</unclear> the spirit: In the first birth, the human's mother is the Earth, for he was made out of her. That is now his mother, and he is not taken according to the first death—she who was made from the rib of Adam—but he is understood to come from the mother Earth. 

Likewise, the other mother here—as we join them—is the water and the spirit. Therefore the pioneer <term>ausspfeher: a scout or one who goes before; here referring to Christ as the one who opens the way</term> Christ was baptized: so whoever is baptized in that same water comes again into the second birth, in exactly the same way as a child lies in the mother's womb; he sets this here as an equivalent. Thus these are conceived and born out of the water; that is now the second mother into which we must enter. 

And he says then of this high matter: that we must be born from above, or we shall not see the kingdom of God. From this you know that baptism is from above—not from man, but from God. Therefore it is uniquely fashioned; the manner of baptism takes the means of the second birth from above, and afterward the Spirit is added. Now the Spirit of which he speaks here is the Spirit of whom Christ reports that He makes alive. That is to say: Christ was conceived and born of the Virgin through the Holy Spirit, and that is the Mother Mary. Thus, in place of Mary, we will lie and be in the water, which is now the baptism; it stands in the place of Mary. And in the same way as Christ was received in the appearance of the Virgin and becomes flesh and blood, so we become the flesh and blood of Christ through the Holy Spirit in the water. For the Spirit in baptism, through the Word, gives flesh and blood from above as a mother; from which it follows that we have these two: the baptism from above as a mother, and the Spirit carries us. We have there the Holy Spirit of the new human birth from above, and both are one Word, for baptism is a Word of Christ. Therefore baptism is as he instituted it to be performed.

### The Spirit blows where it wills. <note>original Latin: "Spiritus ubi vult spirat"</note>

## Nicodemus answered and said to him, "How can these things be?" Jesus answered and said to him, "Are you a teacher in Israel, and you do not know these things? Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know, and we testify to what we have seen. And you do not receive our testimony." <note>John 3:9-11</note>

Thus those who are born of the Spirit become sons, born from the Mother (Baptism) and the Spirit (the Father of the Spirit). In this way, every person is born as a person; just as that same person is divine. Preaching and testimony are held, but he who is of the Spirit is a son of God. He can better speak in the truth. Thus there are true worshippers in Spirit and in truth; "Father, here you are, you who are in Heaven." For He is the cause within them. And He seeks out who His children are, and they come to Him in the resurrection, born from heaven. A person can for once take a body upon themselves, but this is not to be understood naturally as coming from Adam—that is, from the light of nature. 

But because Nicodemus was a master in Israel and learned in the Holy Scriptures, which teach the way of holiness, it is a matter of ignorance <note>original: "Ignoranz"</note>; he should have known and recognized these things. Not from his own human understanding, but as reported through the power of the Scriptures and according to the content of the Spirit. But the prophet <note>likely referring to John the Baptist</note> did not baptize [in this way]; the spokesman <note>original: "barmundt"</note> thinks, "what do I do for the word?" Therefore Christ concluded: what we know, we speak. That is: what I know, I say; and you say what you know. And what I see, I say. I, who hear, tell it to you; and thus everyone testifies to that which he knows and hears. But that which I testify, you do not accept.

Because the Jews did not believe Christ when he told them of human things which everyone had seen, they still did not believe him. Why [should they believe] in such secret knowledge, when obvious things are not believed by everyone?

### And no one has ascended into heaven, except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven. <note>original Latin: "Et nemo ascendit in Coelum, nisi qui descendit de Coelo, Filius hominis qui ē in Coelo."</note>

### And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up: so that everyone who believes in him may not perish, but have eternal life. <note>original Latin: "Et sicut Moses serpentem exaltavit in deserto, ita exaltari oportet filium hoīs: ut oīs q[ui] credit in ipsum, non pereat, sed habeat Vitam aeternam."</note>

For the flesh that is with us has come from heaven, but the [natural] body did not. Now we have them both: namely, the spirit from God the Father, and the body from God the Son.
