Therefore, Christ spoke rightly that it is not [so]. For truly, life is with us, while Christ is with His heavenly Father. All of this must align with the Word of Christ, where He says: "**This is my body, this is my blood.**" Likewise: "**Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.**" He also testifies to this when He speaks: "**The bread that I give you is my flesh.**" And this He gave at the Last Supper. Therefore, it is His body. We must possess that same body so that a **New Creature** may be formed from it.

But now follows this: what use is the flesh? Nothing. But if it is to be of use, then the Spirit must also be present—that is, God. This is the Spirit of whom Christ speaks here. What use is it for a man <note>The original reads "soul," but context suggests "person" or "being."</note> to have a body but no soul? They must both be there. Therefore, we should not only turn [the bread] into flesh, but rely upon it; otherwise, it would be of no use if Christ Himself were not also present there. A man exists beforehand; and when he receives the soul, he must already be flesh; only then does the Spirit or the soul [give life]. So also, when we are born [anew] at the Last Supper, we enter into a new body—this is the conclusion of Christ. But what is it if the Spirit of God is not also given with it? Then we die the eternal death. From this it now follows that Christ is not [locally] present where His body, flesh, and blood are <note>The author argues for a spiritual presence rather than a local, physical one in the bread/wine</note>. # DECLARATION OF THE LORD’S SUPPER. <note>original Latin: *CŒNÆ DOMINI DECLARATIO*</note>

Here, in the description of my purpose regarding the explanation of the Last Supper of our Lord Jesus Christ, it is first most necessary to describe its fruitfulness <note>referring to the spiritual efficacy or benefits of the sacrament</note>. I will describe the manner of it, which contains within it the reason and the specific necessity for eating—not as an excess, but as a necessity—just as we must or should have something in this manner while on this Earth; for we have never eaten [in this way before], so we shall perhaps have eating and drinking in Eternal Life. And once these matters have been so divided, I will then proceed to the interpretation of the text, as its progression shall require.

Just as we are born from Adam unto death in the flesh here [on earth] and hereafter, so are we born from Christ through His flesh and blood unto Eternal Life in heaven. And just as the death of Adam, here on Earth, prepares and establishes a seat for the soul in a mortal or perishable life, so also, in the same manner, from the flesh and blood of Christ, a seat is prepared and made for the soul for salvation in Eternal Life. As in Adam the soul dies the Eternal death along with the mortal flesh, so the soul unites itself with the body of Christ through His flesh and blood for Eternal Life.

And just as the soul of man is nothing alone and noble without the flesh of Adam: so too is that same soul nothing in Eternal Life without the flesh and [blood] of Christ. For the soul and the body on Earth constitute one single thing, and not two separate parts; whatever the one is, the other is also. For in Adam is the Earth; therefore the soul has become mortal, for it has been wedded to the mortal and sinful flesh of the world, and thus also subjected to death. But when it is separated from the Earth, it must be lovely against Death, if it wishes to have life. This, however, occurs through the assistance of much flesh and blood, such as we do not have from Adam. Thus it must happen through Christ alone, whose flesh and earthliness makes the earth within us—both of the body and the soul—unto glory <note>The original term *Erligkeit* likely refers to *Herrlichkeit* (glory) or *Erlösung* (redemption).</note>. Just as no one is redeemed through Adam, nor lives after death [through him]: so no one is [freed] from their sins through him, for through Adam [one stands] before the face of God [in judgment]. Yet his soul has become blessed in the [Redeemer], just as the flesh of the old Adam is restored by way of water and spirit <note>original: *spiritus*</note>, as has happened with the soul. That which has become so blessed has all occurred through the [participation] in the body and soul of Christ. Since the body is given from Christ, outside of whom no one has ever become blessed or holy. And it is only possible if our <margin>B.C.</margin> soul is bodily wedded to the blood and flesh of Christ; otherwise <margin>NB. <note>original Latin abbreviation for *Nota Bene*, meaning "Note Well"</note></margin> there is no salvation in us. But as is now said of this: those who are blessed without such a wedding, such as the Old Fathers <note>the Patriarchs and prophets of the Old Testament</note>...

God made Adam out of clay <term>leymen</term> through His word, and he was a human being. Thus, Adam was born through the word out of the clay. Now, the first birth proceeded from the mouth of God. But the second proceeds from Christ. Instead of the clay, bread is taken; rather, His mouth is the Word which makes the body that Christ put on. Though he was merely a human being made by God the Father in His image, form, and likeness, this birth would no longer be according to that [physical] form, manner, or birth. Instead, it signifies alone the birth of salvation through which we are accepted by God the Father.

For His creation betrayed Him at the "bite" <note>original: "am biß," referring to Adam eating the forbidden fruit</note>, and He came to regret it soon after the fall of Adam. This last word the Son has provided for the second time, and He makes a "bite" <note>The author plays on the word "bite" (biß), comparing the forbidden fruit to the sacramental bread</note> out of His bread, which is His body. From this, we are born for the second time, according to the manner of the birth of Adam, out of God’s word: "Let it be done" <note>original Latin: "Fiat"</note>.

And just as that same birth of Adam was, and happened without a mother’s womb, solely from the mouth of God: so also, as the other birth happened solely through Christ, this flesh of the New Birth—and this blood too—is thus not merely a clothing for Adam (that is, the last creation). For truly, God is before our eyes. For the creature that God has wrought [in the first birth] does not enter into heaven. Now, He does not reject His creation, nor does He destroy it; instead, He lets it remain, though He examines it closely. Nevertheless, it remains. 

But He has never regretted that which is of the second birth; that same thing remains until the end of the world, and it is precisely that through which you are saved. However, that which He regretted <note>the fallen nature of the first creation</note> is not saved. Therefore, there is the second birth. Therefore, take and know this: that the wise should reject the [old] human and all things for the sake of the second creation. For man is born here for the second time, as has been frequently stated. Thus also in this New Birth all things have become new, as Peter speaks and indicates in the book of Acts <note>original: "Acto: 10. v. 15"</note>: "What God has made clean, do not call common."

Since all things have now become new—as is proven by the clear meaning of all your interpretation—He is the second creation, just as the human is in the second birth. Therefore, all the ordinances of the [old] testament are abolished, dead, and set aside.
<margin>(Also, understand the testaments.)</margin>

# Interpretation of the Evangelist St. Mark.

> And while they were eating, Jesus took bread, and having blessed it, he broke it and gave it to them, and said, "Take, this is my body." <note>original Latin: "Et manducantibus illis, accepit Iesus panem, et benedicens fregit ac dedit eis, et ait, sumite hoc est corpus meum."</note>

Thus Mark also speaks with one voice and the same word as Matthew: that Christ took the bread and thanked God his heavenly Father for such great grace—namely, that He entrusted the creature to him, allowing them to be newly admitted into **creation** <note>original: "Schöpfung"</note> and reformed for eternal life. Therefore, this thanksgiving happened rightfully, for according to the will of the Father <margin>(Note:)</margin> that he [Christ] extinguished the Spirit, for which reason he also surrendered his body. For see, the creature was once struck down by God and placed solely upon the Son. Therefore, the Son thanks the Father that He granted, allowed, and permitted him this work of **human creation** <note>original: "Menschöpfung"; likely a compound implying the re-creation or restoration of humanity</note>, so that the poor fallen human race would not be entirely lost and condemned. Therefore He took bread also so that all of us who desire from the heart to be saved should remember him. All of this is beyond our understanding, like supernatural things. And just as he was born of the virgin beyond nature, so too he is released there beyond nature, just as he was in Mary's womb. And both are incomprehensible to human reason.

Afterward he gave it to them and said: "Take and eat, this is my body." This means, in a clear way, just as a child receives its birth according to the form of nature; and just as nature loved, so too he loved me, so that this morsel of bread may be your new body. Just as a seed for children from which a child comes into its form—as it is among you—so is the body that I have taken upon myself for your sake and received, so that I may give it to you, and thus make you according to myself—that is, according to my image. Not from something else, but from myself, so that you may be my children and siblings; [you] shall not be alone, but also [with the] Father. And thus also a **Redeemer** <note>original: "Erlöser"</note> at the same time. In the same way, he also took the **drinking vessel** <note>original: "Trinckgeschirr"; the chalice</note> and commanded them all to drink from it, as in Matthew.

### Interpretation of the Text of St. Luke

Luke records the beginning of the Last Supper more beautifully than the other two Evangelists, for he began and said how Christ spoke to his disciples: "With desire and longing I have desired to eat this Passover with you." That is to say, even before death, He—I have made myself a servant to you and desired of my Father to give you the eternal Supper. That is: Since you are formed in me from the body of the Son, I will make you a creature that is pleasing to my Father.

He had kept this time hidden, from the fall of Adam until here, from Paradise until this Supper. In this we know that man is a double creature <note>The author posits that humans have two "births": the first is physical (from the Father), and the second is spiritual (through the Son).</note>: the first from the Father, and the other from the Son. From this it follows that every creature has its own creaturely food. The body which the Father created eats from the spirit of the Earth from which it came, for flesh finds its like. Just as man was created from the Earth, so all his nourishment—herbs, fruit, and bread—is also created from the Earth. Therefore, man also eats the body out of which he is made, and that is the first birth. But now the second birth involves his God and the last things, as mentioned above; we must nevertheless maintain the natural body and nourish it. But this body, which is created for the second time in a supernatural way...

Having intended this same remembrance—I who am now with you—the remembrance should therefore proceed fully into the **fruit of the Supper**. Where it does not so proceed, there is no power in the remembrance of the Supper. It must happen out of love for Him; for love for Him compels His presence. 

Therefore, know the day—that is: that this evening meal, the Supper, was founded and instituted by Him, and we should keep His ordinance until we go together into His Kingdom. And there, all is a shared remembrance. That is: Not that we have a mere remembrance of Christ, but His power, His might, His love, His faithfulness, His death, suffering, resurrection, and all the benefits He has earned for you thereby. We should think on all of this and recall it in repentance as often as we do it. That is: As often as we observe the bread, the day, the hour, the **action** or **celebration**. For it is not a food that should be taken daily <note>The author distinguishes between "daily bread" for physical survival and the sacramental meal for spiritual life.</note>, but a food that nature—derived from Adam's counsel—cannot consume.

Therefore, because these things wish to be remembered, we should receive Him. Now, however, so that the *textus* [the text] may be well and thoroughly understood, there stands shortly hereafter in the same chapter the following:

### Interpretation of the Text of John, Chapter 6, verse 27

> "Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which remains unto eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you. For this one God the Father has sealed. They said therefore to Him, 'What shall we do, that we may work the work of God?' As has now been said, John did not describe the Supper <note>term: "Nachtmal" (Evening Meal). A common German term for the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note> in the same manner as the three other Evangelists, but rather he alone revealed the nature of the heavenly table. But now to explain it: there is a table on Earth and one in heaven. Only the holy sit at this table. Now, there are not two different kinds of holy people, but only one kind. For there is only one God—namely, the God of the holy. 

However, as I said at the beginning, John did not take note of the testament <note>term: "testament." Here referring to the "Words of Institution" (This is my body, etc.) through which the New Covenant or Testament was established.</note> as it occurred on Earth, and his words should not be dragged into that context. Although it is one and the same food—which might also cause one to eat worthily or sinfully, just as with the sacraments—understand it this way: John does not include the preaching of the heavenly [table]. Whoever wants to understand the heavenly must believe the words of Christ, which were instituted in the testament according to the three other Evangelists. But he who believes the testament to be only an earthly thing does not believe John; thus, they look upon one another as adversaries. And yet, it is one thing of which they all speak together. 

The only difference is that John speaks in the Spirit—that we are to receive that same Word after our death. The three Evangelists, however—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—explain that such a Word is to be received in this life, as is recounted hereafter. Now, it is one food and one drink on both sides, as has been stated. By this, understand the parts together here: the first three Evangelists belong together because they speak of earthly creatures <note>original: "Jrdische Creatur." This refers to the physical elements of bread and wine used in the earthly sacrament.</note> provided through Christ for the Supper.

Therefore, you who are chosen by **God** in **Christ**, distinguish now whether **John** in this chapter, or in his entire Gospel, is [the same as] the other three **Evangelists**. And although he did not include the **Lord’s Supper** within it, nevertheless, dear friends, the **formal words of institution** <note>original Latin: "formalia institutionis"; the specific ritual words "This is my body..."</note> are seen more clearly therein than in the [narrative of the] **Lord’s Supper**. For the time for it had not yet come then. It was just like a preface and a reference to the **Lord’s Supper**, just as **John the Baptist** was a **forerunner** <note>original: "einleuffer," meaning one who runs ahead to announce an arrival.</note> of the Lord **Christ**. And it was a preamble and a teaching for all believers, for this speech subsequently provides the understanding of the **Lord’s Supper**. And what is so gloriously spoken of in this place is the interpretation of that very thing. And that grace which **God the Father** spoke and established in the **institution** <note>The formal establishment of the sacrament.</note> is the glorious interpretation. And although we first heard **John** speaking of the **Lord’s Supper** just as he reported it here, understand it no differently than if I were to say: **John the Baptist** is indeed not **Christ**, but **John** would not have spoken of **Christ** otherwise, nor pointed Him out and proclaimed Him; and he is the **Prophet** who pointed to Him with the finger of **God**. 

Thus, **John the Evangelist** is, in this passage, the interpreter, leader, and predecessor of the **Lord’s Supper**, and he serves as a witness to the **institution** of the same, just as the other three **Evangelists** do. For it was true that at the time of **Christ's** work, the **Lord’s Supper**—for which we take the testimony here—had not yet been instituted or begun, just as it is recounted in the others' accounts of His birth.

# Interpretation of the Text of St. Paul

> <note>original Latin: "Ecce accepi a domino quod et tradidi vobis. Quoniam Dominus Jhesus in ea nocte qua traditus est accepit panem, Et gratias agens fregit et dixit Accipite et manducate hoc est corpus meum quod pro vobis traditur."</note> Behold, I received from the Lord that which I also delivered to you: That the Lord Jesus, on the night in which he was betrayed, took bread, and giving thanks, broke it and said, "Take and eat; this is my body which is given for you."

St. Paul has diligently undertaken to describe and explain the **Lord’s Supper** <note>original: "Nachtmal," literally "night-meal."</note> so that he might teach that the second article of faith <note>The second article of the Apostles' Creed, which focuses on Jesus Christ’s suffering and sacrifice.</note> remains preserved. He intends to lead us to faith and concludes that we truly possess the Body and Blood of Christ there, according to the explicit words of Christ. We should not cast this into doubt or seek alternative interpretations; rather, he confirms and explains the history step-by-step for the specific and certain comfort of our conscience, so that we do not waver. He did not merely discuss this, but set it down with such precision that Christ’s words would be easier to understand. He remains consistent with the beginning of the ritual, Christ's thanksgiving, the breaking of bread, and the conclusion with those same words—"Mine"—following the exact order of the three Evangelists: Matthew, Mark, and Luke. He also says: **"As often as you do this, do it in my remembrance."** From this, the following words are further understood: **"As often as you do this, you shall proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes in his Glory."**

Thus, the three Evangelists are understood through Paul in this passage. As often as we do this, we shall proclaim and remember the Lord’s death. This is the remembrance we are to perform until He returns in His **Glory** <note>original: "Gloria"</note>. That is, when we shall be in His Father’s Kingdom. At that time, He will come to the **Procession** <unclear>Procession</unclear> <note>original: "Proceß." This likely refers to the "judicial proceedings" of the Last Judgment or the triumphal "procession" of Christ's return.</note>, and we shall go to Him. Know from this that we should observe the **Lord’s Supper** in the same manner as described before, without the slightest change. And once this has been done, we should proclaim the death of the Lord in our hearts—not just with the mouth—as a memorial to Him. This is for us and for our benefit; as the words to the angel of **Philadelphia** <note>A reference to the faithful church mentioned in Revelation 3:7-13.</note> clarify, He suffered and acted solely for our sake. He has surrendered Himself—that is, ordained in a **Testament** <note>term: "Testament" — used here to mean both a "Last Will and Testament" and the "Covenant" of the New Testament.</note> for these times—for us to partake of His body, His true body, and His blood. He commanded such service by the power of divine authority, in a different manner than other commandments. This is the highest commandment in the Testament. Whoever does not live according to it does not proclaim the death of the Lord. For Christ desires that we observe His supper and thereby proclaim His death.

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of the Lord’s Supper, moving from the human understanding of Paul’s words to the distinction between "worldly" substance and the "spiritual-bodily" presence of Christ in the sacrament. Know that there is a distinction between what the world gives—which is the dead and worldly—and what the earth does not give, which is spiritual; for it is God who gives it. And in a way, they do not see it as a worldly thing. What the earth does not give is spiritual, for God gives it; therefore it is so. Consider that it is gathered together like a spirit, which no manner of eating or grasping can reach. Thus, it bears the name "spiritual" here, and yet it is not a spirit, but a body and blood. Yet, He was not yet physically present. Likewise, that food was not yet anything physical. But through the **Lord’s Supper** <note>original: "Nachtmal." Literally "Night-meal," the standard term for the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note> they hoped for what would come afterward. Therefore, they received it spiritually, because it was not yet there. Thus, they did not enjoy it bodily for their own part, but spiritually. For what is lost in **Adam** <note>The fallen, mortal nature of humanity.</note> is henceforth like a spirit, yet a bodily spirit.

And it is not an incorporeal spirit, but this spirit-nature is internal and bodily. Had they possessed it—since they were also mortal—they would not have eaten in a way that leads to death. Therefore, on their part, it was spiritual, and not for the sake of the food, which is eaten as if it were nothing internal. Their spirit also ate Christ bodily, and yet softly as if on Earth. For they [knew] what was to happen, whereas the others lacked that expectation. From this, know that I may say: I receive the Lord’s Supper spiritually—that is, I eat the flesh and drink His blood—yet I do not see it. Therefore, it is as much as a bodily spirit, in a manner that can be thrust outward, passing through masonry and through walls. And they are meanwhile physically present in the mouth, just as Christ was. 

Thus I also receive it spiritually, for **Adam’s body** <note>The physical, corruptible body of man.</note> is of no use in this; it goes to the gates of the earth. In a way, however, they also had it from Him through all walls. This is what the spirit should understand in this manner: a bodily spirit is the spirit that is the person who is blood and flesh. But it is **transformed** <note>original: "Conficiert." Derived from the Latin *conficere*, referring to the consecration or the spiritual "making" of the sacramental elements.</note>. For in a way, they [the elements] are held within closed walls, between partitions, so the flesh remains there; and in a way they do not see that eternal love is fastened through all walls and is thrust toward God, just as Christ came out of the grave, through the sealed stone, through walls and closed doors. And yet He was no spirit, but a true body. Whoever possesses understanding believes that what is called a "pure spirit" is otherwise rightly acknowledged as a spirit and blood-filled flesh, which was once handled; that is what belongs to the high spirit. <meta>This page continues the theological exploration of the Lord’s Supper, specifically examining the Apostle Paul’s writings in 1 Corinthians. It transitions from the historical experience of the Patriarchs to a defense of the literal "Real Presence" of Christ in the bread and wine, contrasting this with those who view the sacrament as merely symbolic.</meta>

He introduces yet another discourse and says: **"I speak to the wise; judge for yourselves what I say."** <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 10:15.</note> He addresses those who use their own understanding—their high-minded "shrewdness" and the spirit of the **highly-learned** <note>original: "Hochgeliehrten." This refers to academic theologians who rely on reason over faith.</note>—regarding this high article of faith. They wish to be wiser than God Himself and His Apostles. These are precisely the ones who interpret the Word of God without being called to do so; instead, they appoint themselves so that they might be highly regarded by the world. 

Therefore, they allow many things into their understanding—in this matter and in that—saying, "The Lord says this," and "The Lord says that," simply to stop the mouths of their neighbors. Yet it should be as Paul says: **"For you shall not muzzle the mouth of the ox while it treads out the grain,"** <note>1 Corinthians 9:9 and 1 Timothy 5:18. The author is applying the metaphor of the working ox to those truly called to preach.</note> etc. They should not be hindered in their calling but left free; that is, they should not be enchanted with deceit, but rather, the one who is called should honor God.

Now, where he says, **"The cup of blessing which we bless,"** he follows the tradition of the Apostles. **"Is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?"** <note>1 Corinthians 10:16.</note> This means: Christ has given His precious blood to be drunk. Therefore, is that which we bless not that very same blood? For **communion** <term>fellowship or shared participation; original: "gemeinschaft"</term> is nothing other than being of one kind, not of two different kinds; it is that same blood of Christ. The blood in our hand is a "communion"—that is, it is one blood. The same is true of the bread that we break. When is it broken? In the preaching and the human act, not just in faith or in the spirit; it is physical food and drink. Since we now break the bread, it is just as much the bread that Christ Himself broke.

Here, one must ask whether Paul does not follow the words of the **Evangelists** <note>The Gospel writers: Matthew, Mark, and Luke.</note> and wish to bless as they did. For everything beyond this is contention. Long ago, there were heretics among the Corinthians who shaped their faith in the same way as those in our own times. To them, there is nothing physical, only what is in faith. Just as we say "spirit," they say "only a void"; just as we say "teaching," they say "wind." 

But Paul wishes to introduce nothing else; he remains simply by the clear words as the letter sounds. He remains on the foundation of how Christ acted and spoke at the **Last Supper** <note>original: "Abendtmal."</note> and brings nothing foreign into it, such as saying it is "not physical" etc. Instead, he speaks plainly: It is a word. It is not "only a symbol" (as the superior <term>Enthusiasts</term> <note>original: "schwermer." A derogatory term used by Luther and others for radical reformers who believed the bread and wine were only symbols.</note> inappropriately say against the clear words of the institution). They say, "In this way you eat Him," or "Faith is the eating," or "He must be eaten in the heart." But the Apostle holds fast to the fact that it is truly He. Even if it were asked how so many of you can each eat a part, that does not break the unity; it is merely distributed in pieces. 

But listen to this discourse: **"We are all one bread and one body,"** <note>1 Corinthians 10:17.</note> which means we are all born out of Christ from one **source.** <note>original: "Limbo." Here used not to mean the theological "Limbo of the Fathers," but rather the "origin" or "common womb" of spiritual life.</note> Thus, we have only one body and likewise only one food, and it is not divided. Since Paul preaches so clearly here and does not press any other interpretation, but remains moderate within the pure text, how can wise men possibly [resist] the same...

# THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS'S EXPLANATION
## OF THE ANGELIC SALUTATION.

A human being can never understand with **reason** how a young virgin became pregnant by the Holy Spirit without a man. Therefore, we must let it rest upon what the Angel said, and not trouble ourselves further with it. We cannot think it out any further. <margin>Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book 1: He gave man a sublime face and ordered him to look at the sky, and to lift his upright countenance to the stars. <note>original: "Os homini sublime dedit (cœlumque tueri iussit, et erectos ad sidera tollere Vultus."</note></margin> <margin>Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods: God raised man up from the ground and made him tall and upright, so that he might look toward heaven, as if toward his former home and kindred. <note>original: "DEus hominem humo excitatum, celsos erectos constituit, ad cœlũque, quasi cognationis domiciliÿque pristini conspectum, excitavit."</note></margin>

Now look at the **Phoenix**, which is a truly fiery bird; does it not represent Christ hanging on the Cross for us? <note>In medieval and Renaissance thought, the Phoenix was a common symbol for the Resurrection, as it dies in fire and is reborn from the ashes.</note>
Furthermore, look at the **Sun**; does it not depict for us the Divine Trinity through its body, its form, and its heat?
Observe the **three prime matters** <term>Tria Prima: The three fundamental alchemical principles—Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury—which Paracelsus believed composed all things.</term> in the analysis of all plants and juices; do you not find the Most Holy Trinity there through the **Spagyric art**? <term>Spagyric: A term coined by Paracelsus for alchemical medicine-making, involving the separation of a substance's components and their subsequent purification and recombination.</term>

For He purifies, illuminates, and regenerates his "bones"—just as one purifies other imperfect metals into **Gold**—and makes them fit and constant for the **battle of FIRE**.

Now observe: how are these metallic spirits born in the Light of Nature? In the same way as is written above in Luke, Chapter 1, Verse 35, from the mouth of the Angel Gabriel. For the "Power of the Highest," that is, God...

Yet beyond all this, He must be a Son of the Most High; therefore, the Most High, born from the beginning, later "hatched" <note>The German "ausgebruet" implies a slow, vital warmth, much like an alchemist warming a flask or a bird on an egg.</note> Him into a spiritual and divine body within the Middle Body, and from the Middle Body He was embalmed, seasoned, and made into a whole Christ, who is true God and man. 

But what is the "patient" Middle Body? A pure, chaste virgin whom no man has ever defiled. For into this our secret and high work (as the truly wise say), nothing foreign enters. This birth proceeds from only one **Matter**, which has no husband except for its own spirit and soul to create it. The coming Spirit <note>original: "Spiritus superveniens"</note> is God the Most High, and He provides this handmaid with her husband: and from the seed she conceives, and afterwards bears the Son of the Most High. And because He is a Son of the Most High, the **highest eternal center** <note>original: "Centrum eternum"</note> lies within Him. For no one knows the Father but the Son.

# Preparation of Salts for the preparation of <unclear>Gold</unclear> so that it remains in the Cupel like Gold <note>original: $\odot$; the symbol for the Sun and Gold. A "capella" or cupel is a shallow, porous vessel used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals.</note>

Let the best pulverized ingredients be mixed in a strong mill and very well <unclear>ground</unclear>, and let them be reverberated <note>original: *reverberentur*; heated in a reverberatory furnace where the flame is deflected or "reverberated" onto the material.</note> for 9 or 12 hours. Afterward, increase the fire until that <unclear>fused substance</unclear> grows red; then [reduce it] into powder and you will have the Salt, which you should save.

Afterward, take 1 part of the Sal Ammoniac which you have with strong vitriol <note>original: *vitriolo*; a sulfate mineral, likely used here to create a corrosive acid.</note>, and distill it; and being fixed by a very slow fire, let it be <unclear>set</unclear> and purified.

<margin>With this salt <note>original: $\ominus$</note> prepared and <unclear>completed</unclear></margin>
From those salts, you will have a most potent and most purified salt <note>original: $\ominus$</note>. Then let them be mixed together upon strong Plates <note>original: *Laminis*; thin sheets of metal.</note> so that the value of both is coagulated into one. Then take these strong bodies:

Make a layer of the vessels and these [salts], then with your salt, let it be placed so that the layer is thick enough; apply the Plates, then the Salts, <unclear>thickly</unclear> (and do this until the vessel is <unclear>full</unclear>). Seal it with lute <note>original: *Luta*; a clay or cement used to make vessels airtight.</note> and place it in the fire: for 8 or 10 or 12 hours, giving it a good fire, as much or more than for <unclear>melting</unclear> metals, provided the Furnace <note>original: *Caminus*</note> is <unclear>closed</unclear> with a roof; then by the blasts of the furnace, let it remain until 9 <unclear>parts</unclear> remain, always with the roof secured.

Perform the fire of fusion <note>Heating until the substance melts.</note>: then the entire property will depart from your remaining material (because they are <unclear>refined</unclear>). After the preparation, wash it in powder; therefore obtain that [substance] with the water of the Salt. This provides firmness, and you shall lose nothing of the power. <unclear>The Lord be with your art</unclear>.

### The third point in this disputation of Christ with the Jews to be understood.

Therefore the Jew will not let God be praised in everything, so that
he understands Christ's speech from them: also many go away from
him, whom he wanted for his disciples, also they [went] away from me.
Though Christ is rightly presented, he will sigh, that he
became the one who, for the sake of the words, wanted to **fall away**
**from you.** For You have the word that is living. Now it is
he as if the sinner spoke. Why should we yield from you,
yield and leave [you]: I [know] that you have that which gives us eternal life.
From this it also follows that they [yield] to him, for that is no one right.
You are the Christ the Son of God: It is indeed God the unbelievable.
But he wants it understood thus, that they have from God, 
not being praised by God when they waver. <margin>v. 70.</margin> Therefore he
says. The Apostles are indeed in him: for God has
praised them. From one among them, namely Judas, who was not praised before God.
